candidates.title: Molecular orbitals & conjugation
candidates.interaction: Snap carbon atoms into chains and rings to build a π system (ethene, butadiene, benzene, cyclobutadiene, a cyanine dye); the page diagonalizes the Hückel matrix and draws the molecular orbitals as signed lobes on the atoms beside an energy ladder filled with the π electrons. Lengthen a dye chain and watch the HOMO-LUMO gap shrink while a swatch shows the color it absorbs; close a chain into a ring and watch the levels regroup into the aromatic pattern, or fail to for a four-membered ring.
candidates.takeaway: Electrons delocalized over a π system fill a ladder of orbitals whose gap narrows as the system grows, which is why longer dyes are redder and why a six-membered ring is stable where a four-membered one is not.
candidates.needs: Measured absorption maxima of a cyanine dye series for the color panel, to set beside the computed gap.
candidates.pitfall: Benzene's bonds do not alternate between single and double; the orbitals spread over the whole ring, and the two Kekulé drawings are a convention, not structures it flips between.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 5.61 Physical Chemistry devotes Lecture 26 to qualitative MO theory (Hückel): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-61-physical-chemistry-fall-2017/resources/qualitative-mo-theory-huckel/
candidates.overlapWith: chemical-bonds: that page builds molecules from localized electron pairs and VSEPR shapes; this one computes delocalized orbital energies and shapes from the Hückel Hamiltonian.
candidates.needsSource: Published λmax values of the classic cyanine dye series (literature numbers, not a licensed dataset); the Hückel model itself needs no data.

candidates.title: Hartree-Fock: the self-consistent field
candidates.interaction: Step through a self-consistent-field calculation on H2 or HeH+ in a minimal basis: start from a guessed orbital, build the Fock matrix from it, solve, and watch the orbitals, the electron density and the energy settle iteration by iteration until the field the electrons make is the field they were solved in. Then drag the bond length to trace the energy curve, and switch on the exact two-determinant answer in the same basis to see the mean-field curve go wrong as the bond breaks.
candidates.takeaway: Each electron is solved in the average field of the others and the loop repeats until nothing changes, which captures most of the bond but misses the correlation between electrons that matters most when a bond is pulled apart.
candidates.needs: STO-3G exponents and contraction coefficients for H and He; all integrals are computed in the browser.
candidates.pitfall: Exchange is not a force between electrons, and the Hartree-Fock energy is an upper bound: the missing correlation energy is small per electron but is exactly what a stretched bond needs.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 5.61 covers molecular orbital theory, and the Szabo & Ostlund HeH+ SCF program is the standard worked example (CCL archive): https://ccl.net/cca/software/SOURCES/FORTRAN/szabo/index.html
candidates.overlapWith: huckel-molecular-orbitals (proposed): Hückel takes the matrix elements as parameters; this page computes them from the electrons' own repulsion and iterates to self-consistency.
candidates.needsSource: STO-3G parameters from the Basis Set Exchange (MolSSI, openly licensed; confirm the current licence) or as printed in Szabo & Ostlund (a dozen numbers).

candidates.title: Molecular vibrations: IR & Raman
candidates.interaction: Assemble a small molecule (HCl, CO2, H2O, CH4) from atoms and bond springs with real force constants; the page diagonalizes the Hessian and animates each normal mode. For each mode it tests whether the vibration changes the molecule's dipole or its polarizability and draws the predicted IR and Raman stick spectra next to measured line positions; swap an atom for a heavier isotope and the peaks shift.
candidates.takeaway: A molecule's IR spectrum is the set of its vibration frequencies, fixed by bond stiffness and atom masses, and a vibration appears in IR only if it moves charge and in Raman only if it changes polarizability, so CO2's symmetric stretch is silent in one and bright in the other.
candidates.needs: Harmonic force constants for the molecules (Herzberg's tabulations) and measured band positions for comparison.
candidates.pitfall: CO2 is a greenhouse gas because its bend and asymmetric stretch change its dipole, not because it is a gas that traps heat; N2 and O2 vibrate too but stay invisible in IR.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 5.61 covers molecular spectroscopy, and OCR/AQA A-level chemistry assess IR spectra with an absorption data sheet: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-61-physical-chemistry-fall-2017/
candidates.overlapWith: greenhouse-effect: that page takes absorption as an input; this one computes which vibrations absorb and why from the molecule's own mechanics.
candidates.needsSource: HITRAN line lists for CO2, H2O, HCl and CH4 (free with citation per hitran.org; the 1986 edition mirror at NCAR is CC BY 4.0). NIST WebBook IR spectra are free to view but their redistribution terms are not clearly open, so the page should rely on HITRAN.

candidates.title: NMR: spins, pulses & spectra
candidates.interaction: Put nuclear spins in a magnetic field, fire a 90° pulse and watch the net magnetization tip and precess while the detector records the decaying signal, then Fourier-transform it into a peak. Add a second spin with a scalar coupling and the peak splits into a doublet; set real chemical shifts for ethanol's three environments and watch the whole spectrum assemble, with linewidth following the decay rate.
candidates.takeaway: An NMR spectrometer listens to nuclei precessing after a pulse, and each nucleus's note is shifted by its electron surroundings and split by its neighbours, so the spectrum reads out the molecule's structure.
candidates.needs: Chemical shifts and coupling constants for a few molecules (ethanol, ethyl acetate).
candidates.pitfall: The spectrum is not scanned one frequency at a time; it is the Fourier transform of one decaying signal, and 'spin' does not mean the nucleus is physically spinning like a top.
candidates.why: OCR A-level Chemistry A (H432) module 6 includes proton and carbon-13 NMR with a chemical-shift data sheet: https://www.savemyexams.com/learning-hub/exam-specifications/a-level/chemistry/ocr/
candidates.overlapWith: medical-imaging: that page closes with MRI in a sentence; this one simulates the spin physics behind the signal and reads chemistry from it.
candidates.needsSource: nmrshiftdb2 (University of Cologne), published under an open-content licence as stated on its site (no named CC licence; confirm), or literature shift values.

candidates.title: Fluorescence, phosphorescence & photochemistry
candidates.interaction: Shine a light pulse on a population of molecules shown on a Jablonski ladder and watch them climb and then leave the excited state by competing routes (fluorescence, internal conversion, intersystem crossing, phosphorescence), each with a rate constant on a slider. A plot of emitted light against time shows the lifetime and quantum yield; switch the lamp off to see the slow phosphorescent tail, and add a quencher to watch the Stern-Volmer line steepen.
candidates.takeaway: After absorbing a photon a molecule has several exits with different speeds, and how bright and how long it glows is decided by that race.
candidates.needs: Rate constants, lifetimes and quantum yields for a couple of real fluorophores.
candidates.pitfall: Fluorescence is not reflection and not stored light: the emitted photon carries less energy than the absorbed one because some was lost as heat first (the Stokes shift).
candidates.why: MIT OCW 5.61's syllabus ends with molecular spectroscopy and photochemistry: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/chemistry/5-61-physical-chemistry-fall-2017/index.htm
candidates.overlapWith: vision-color: that page mixes light in the eye; this one models what one molecule does with a photon after absorbing it.
candidates.needsSource: Published lifetimes and quantum yields (e.g. fluorescein, anthracene) from the literature; numbers only, no licensed dataset.

candidates.title: Free energy of mixing & phase diagrams
candidates.interaction: Drag the interaction energy and the temperature of a two-component regular solution and watch its free-energy curve bend; wherever a common tangent lies below the curve the page draws it and splits the mixture into two phases at the tangent points. Sweep the temperature and the phase diagram assembles underneath (miscibility gap and spinodal); add solid and liquid curves to build lens and eutectic diagrams, and drag a composition to read the lever rule.
candidates.takeaway: A phase diagram is the shadow of free-energy curves: a mixture splits wherever a straight line between two compositions lies below the curve, and the tangent points become the phase boundaries.
candidates.pitfall: A two-phase region on a phase diagram is not a phase; the mixture there is two phases of the boundary compositions, in amounts the lever rule gives.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 3.012 problem set 6 builds phase diagrams from common tangents on free-energy curves: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-012-fundamentals-of-materials-science-fall-2005/2cbcd5557e2886b8ce70445f8312394b_ps06_sol.pdf
candidates.overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page tracks one substance on a pressure-temperature diagram; this one derives a two-component diagram from free energy.

candidates.title: Free energy & the equilibrium constant
candidates.interaction: Drag the extent of a reaction (N2O4 ⇌ 2 NO2, with real enthalpy and entropy) along a plot of the mixture's Gibbs energy and watch it fall to a minimum part-way, where the composition matches the equilibrium constant; switch off the mixing-entropy term that bends the curve to see why the reaction would otherwise run to completion. Change the temperature and the pressure and watch the minimum, K and the yield move.
candidates.takeaway: A reaction runs downhill in free energy and stops at the bottom of a curve that lies at a mixture rather than at completion, because mixing itself lowers the free energy; the depth of that bottom is the equilibrium constant.
candidates.needs: Standard enthalpies of formation and entropies for N2O4 and NO2.
candidates.pitfall: A negative ΔG° does not mean the reaction goes to completion and a positive one does not mean it does not happen; the sign sets K, and the mixture always settles at a minimum between the two extremes.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 5.60 Thermodynamics & Kinetics covers chemical equilibrium of gas- and solution-phase reactions through the Gibbs energy: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-60-thermodynamics-kinetics-spring-2008
candidates.overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page reaches equilibrium kinetically, as equal forward and reverse rates; this one locates it thermodynamically as the minimum of G and ties it to K and temperature.
candidates.needsSource: NIST-JANAF thermochemical tables (NIST Standard Reference Data, free to use with citation; a few numbers).

candidates.title: Electrode kinetics: Nernst to Butler-Volmer
candidates.interaction: Set the potential of an electrode in a solution of a redox couple and watch the concentration ratio at its surface follow the Nernst equation while the current follows the Butler-Volmer curve, with a Tafel plot alongside. A diffusion layer in front of the electrode is computed on a grid, so sweeping the potential up and down traces a cyclic voltammogram whose peaks grow with the sweep rate, and pushing too hard shows the current starve as molecules cannot arrive fast enough.
candidates.takeaway: The electrode potential sets the ratio of oxidized to reduced molecules at the surface, and the current is set by how far you push from that balance, until diffusion caps it.
candidates.pitfall: The Nernst equation gives a cell's voltage with no current flowing; under load the voltage is lower by the overpotentials, and current is not the speed of the electrons.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 10.626 Electrochemical Energy Systems covers the thermodynamics, reaction kinetics and transport of electrochemical cells: https://www.ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-626-electrochemical-energy-systems-spring-2014/pages/syllabus
candidates.overlapWith: redox-batteries: that page follows ions and electrons through a lithium cell; this one models the interface itself, how potential sets composition and current.
candidates.needsSource: none (a textbook couple such as ferri/ferrocyanide with literature rate constants)

candidates.title: Corrosion: why iron rusts and zinc saves it
candidates.interaction: Drag a point over the potential-pH map of iron in water, computed live from the Nernst lines of its species, and see which form is stable there: bare metal, dissolved ions or a protective oxide. Couple the iron to a second metal (zinc, copper, tin) and the mixed-potential diagram shows where the two electrode curves cross and which metal dissolves; change the oxygen level, pH or salt content and watch the corrosion current move.
candidates.takeaway: Whether a metal corrodes depends on pH and potential together, and sacrificial zinc protects steel by pulling its potential into the region where iron stays metal.
candidates.needs: Standard potentials and free energies of formation for the iron, zinc, copper and tin species in water, and exchange current densities for the mixed-potential diagram.
candidates.pitfall: Rusting is not iron simply reacting with air: it is an electrochemical cell with anodic and cathodic spots on the same piece of metal, which is why salt water speeds it up so much.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 10.626 Lecture 2 builds cell thermodynamics from the Nernst equation, the basis of Pourbaix and Evans diagrams: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/chemical-engineering/10-626-electrochemical-energy-systems-spring-2014/lecture-notes/MIT10_626S14_Lec2.pdf
candidates.overlapWith: electrode-kinetics (proposed): that page holds one electrode under control; this one lets two reactions on the same metal find their own potential and maps the outcome over pH.
candidates.needsSource: ΔG°f and standard potentials from the NBS tables of chemical thermodynamic properties (Wagman et al. 1982, a US-government compilation; confirm redistribution terms) or equivalent NIST data; exchange current densities from the literature. The Pourbaix Atlas itself is copyrighted and not needed: the lines are computed.

candidates.title: X-ray diffraction: reading a crystal
candidates.interaction: Pick a real crystal structure (NaCl, CsCl, diamond, copper, silicon) and the page computes its structure factors and draws the powder pattern against angle from Bragg's law and the atomic scattering factors; rotate a single crystal to see the spots of its reciprocal lattice pass through the Ewald sphere. Edit the cell by swapping an atom, deleting one or changing the lattice type, and watch peaks appear, vanish or shift; change the X-ray wavelength and the whole pattern rescales.
candidates.takeaway: A diffraction pattern is the crystal's Fourier transform: peak positions come from the spacing of the lattice and peak intensities from where the atoms sit in the cell, so the missing peaks are as telling as the present ones.
candidates.needs: CIF files for the structures and atomic scattering-factor coefficients.
candidates.pitfall: Bragg 'reflection' is not a mirror bouncing a beam off a plane: every atom scatters in all directions and the peaks are where those waves add up, which is why intensities depend on the atoms and not only on the planes.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 3.091 Fall 2018 runs through crystallography and x-rays: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-091-introduction-to-solid-state-chemistry-fall-2018/pages/syllabus/
candidates.overlapWith: semiconductors: that page shows lattices beside their bands; this one computes what X-rays see in a lattice and how structures are solved from it.
candidates.needsSource: Crystallography Open Database entries (COD states they are free to download, reuse and redistribute; confirm its public-domain statement on crystallography.net); scattering factors from the Waasmaier-Kirfel or Cromer-Mann parameterisations as redistributed in BSD-licensed xraylib (the International Tables themselves are copyrighted).

candidates.title: Reaction trajectories & the transition state
candidates.interaction: Fire a classical trajectory of A + BC → AB + C across a potential-energy surface (LEPS model of H + H2 and F + H2) drawn as a contour map, choosing how much energy goes into translation and how much into vibration, and see whether it crosses the saddle or turns back. Sweep the temperature to watch the Eyring rate climb, move the barrier early or late along the path to see which kind of energy gets molecules over it, and swap H for D to watch the zero-point energy and the rate change.
candidates.takeaway: A reaction is a journey over a mountain pass on an energy landscape; the pass's height sets how often molecules make it and its position sets which kind of energy gets them over.
candidates.needs: LEPS (Sato) parameters for the H3 and FH2 surfaces.
candidates.pitfall: The transition state is not an intermediate that can be isolated; it is the top of the pass, crossed in a single vibration, and a catalyst lowers the pass rather than pushing molecules over it.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 5.60 covers rates of chemical reactions and transition-state theory (Lectures 33-35): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-60-thermodynamics-kinetics-spring-2008/resources/lec33_th
candidates.overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page draws a 1D energy profile beside colliding balls; this one computes the 2D surface and real trajectories over it, with the isotope effect as a bonus.
candidates.needsSource: Published LEPS/Sato parameters for H + H2 and F + H2 (journal numbers; no licensed dataset).

candidates.title: Catalysis on a surface
candidates.interaction: Run CO oxidation on a lattice of catalyst sites: CO lands on one empty site, O2 splits onto two neighbouring sites, and adjacent CO and O react into CO2 and leave (the Ziff-Gulari-Barshad model). Slide the CO fraction in the gas and watch the CO2 rate rise, peak and collapse as the surface smothers in CO, with the coverages plotted beside a Langmuir isotherm; raise the temperature to let CO desorb and the dead surface recover.
candidates.takeaway: A catalyst works by holding the reactants next to each other on its surface, and too much of one reactant can cover every site and stop the reaction entirely.
candidates.pitfall: A catalyst is not consumed, but it is not inert either: its activity depends on what covers it, and a poisoned surface is a catalyst that has stopped working.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 10.37 Chemical and Biological Reaction Engineering covers heterogeneous catalysis and Langmuir-Hinshelwood kinetics: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/10-37-chemical-and-biological-reaction-engineering-spring-2007/pages/lecture-notes
candidates.overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page's catalyst only lowers a barrier; this one models the surface sites, their coverage and the poisoning that follows.

candidates.title: Enzyme kinetics
candidates.interaction: Watch one enzyme molecule bind substrate, convert it and release product as a random sequence of events while a thousand copies beside it build the smooth rate curve; slide the substrate concentration and see the rate saturate at Vmax with Km read off at half-height. Add a competitive or a non-competitive inhibitor and watch the curve and its Lineweaver-Burk line change in different ways; load real Km and kcat values for enzymes from carbonic anhydrase to catalase.
candidates.takeaway: An enzyme's rate climbs with substrate only until every enzyme is busy, so the plateau measures the enzyme's speed and the half-way point its grip on the substrate, and an inhibitor reveals which of the two it attacks.
candidates.needs: Km and kcat values for a handful of enzymes.
candidates.pitfall: Vmax is never reached, only approached, and Km is not simply the binding constant: it also contains the catalytic rate.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 5.60 Lecture 35 (enzyme catalysis: Michaelis-Menten and Lineweaver-Burk) and 5.07 session 4: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/5-60-thermodynamics-kinetics-spring-2008/resources/5_60_lecture35
candidates.overlapWith: respiration-atp: that page follows one glucose through the pathways; this one models how fast any enzyme works and what limits it.

candidates.title: Rubber & polymer chains: the entropic spring
candidates.interaction: Grab the ends of a freely-jointed chain of a few hundred links and pull; the page samples the chain's random walks and shows the count of shapes that fit each end-to-end distance collapsing, with the restoring force computed from that count and the temperature. Turn up the temperature and the stretched chain pulls harder and shortens; cross-link many chains into a network and rubber's stress-strain curve appears beside Hooke's law, with the warming on stretching shown on a thermometer.
candidates.takeaway: Rubber pulls back not because its bonds are stretched but because a stretched chain has fewer shapes to be in, so it pulls harder when hotter and warms when stretched, the opposite of a metal spring.
candidates.pitfall: The force in rubber is entropic, not from stretched bonds: a rubber band heated under a weight contracts, which a steel spring never does.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 3.064 Polymer Engineering lecture on chain conformation and the kinetic theory of rubber elasticity (and Feynman's much-shared rubber-band clip): https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-064-polymer-engineering-fall-2003/resources/lec_6
candidates.overlapWith: carbon-polymers: that page links monomers and relates stiffness to chain length and cross-links; this one derives the restoring force from the statistics of a chain's shapes.

candidates.title: Liquid crystals & the LCD pixel
candidates.interaction: Run a lattice of rod-like molecules (Lebwohl-Lasher Monte Carlo) and slide the temperature: above a point the rods point every way, below it they agree on a direction and the order parameter jumps. Apply a voltage across the cell and watch the rods swing toward the field; place the twisted cell between crossed polarizers and the page computes the light that gets through, so the pixel goes from bright to dark as the voltage rises.
candidates.takeaway: A liquid crystal is a liquid whose molecules agree on a direction, and a small voltage re-aims them, which turns a pixel from light to dark in front of a backlight.
candidates.pitfall: The liquid crystal in a screen emits no light; it is a voltage-controlled shutter, and the colors come from filters over a white backlight.
candidates.why: TU/e 'Polymer and colloid science' covers liquid-crystal phases and Onsager theory, and EngineerGuy's LCD teardown is a widely shared explainer: https://eduxchange.nl/ewuu/guest/catalog-tue/courses/polymer-and-colloid-science_300b6aa7-1f16-46f4-be98-05e87310000a
candidates.overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page has solid, liquid and gas; this one adds the state between liquid and crystal and the device built on it.

candidates.title: Glass: the liquid that ran out of time
candidates.interaction: Cool a box of two sizes of simulated atoms at a rate the reader chooses and watch the volume-temperature plot: cooled slowly, a pure sample snaps into a crystal with a sharp drop; cooled quickly, or mixed, it jams into a glass at a gentle kink whose temperature rises with the cooling rate. A mean-squared-displacement plot shows the atoms caging each other as the glass forms, and a structure panel compares the crystal's repeating rows with the glass's frozen liquid.
candidates.takeaway: A glass is a liquid cooled too fast to crystallize, so its atoms jam where they stand, and the temperature where that happens depends on how fast it was cooled.
candidates.pitfall: Window glass does not flow at room temperature; old panes are thicker at one edge because of how they were made, not because the glass sagged.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 3.091 Fall 2018 syllabus includes glasses after crystals and defects: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-091-introduction-to-solid-state-chemistry-fall-2018/pages/syllabus/
candidates.overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page freezes a box into a crystal; this one cools a mixture fast enough that it cannot, and shows what forms instead.

candidates.title: Superconductors
candidates.interaction: Drag the temperature of a slab of superconductor through its critical point while a Ginzburg-Landau order parameter is solved on a grid: above it a magnetic field passes straight through, below it the field is pushed out and a magnet floats above the slab with the computed force. Raise the applied field and watch flux punch in as quantized vortices that pin and hold the magnet in place; compare with a perfect conductor, which keeps whatever field it was cooled in.
candidates.takeaway: Below its critical temperature a superconductor's electrons form one coherent wave that expels magnetic fields and carries current with no resistance, until the field is strong enough to enter as quantized vortices.
candidates.pitfall: A superconductor is not merely a perfect conductor: a perfect conductor would freeze in the field it was cooled with, whereas a superconductor expels it, and the levitation that locks a magnet in place comes from trapped vortices, not from repulsion alone.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 6.763 Applied Superconductivity (London equations, perfect diamagnetism, BCS); the 2023 LK-99 episode showed the public appetite: https://www.ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-763-applied-superconductivity-fall-2005/pages/lecture-notes/
candidates.overlapWith: semiconductors: that page explains conduction through bands and doping; this one models the state where resistance vanishes and fields are expelled.
candidates.needsSource: none (phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau model on a grid; the BCS mechanism is summarized, not simulated, and the page says so)

candidates.title: Quantum dots: color from size
candidates.interaction: Slide the radius of a semiconductor nanocrystal from 2 to 10 nm and the page solves the confinement energy of its electron and hole, adds the bulk band gap and shows the color it emits, next to a ladder of discrete levels that spreads as the dot shrinks. Switch the material and compare the computed emission with measured peak wavelengths of real dots; a density-of-states panel shows the smooth bulk band breaking into sharp levels as the box closes in.
candidates.takeaway: Trap an electron in a box a few nanometres wide and the energy it gives back as light is set by the size of the box, so one material glows in every color depending on how small it is made.
candidates.needs: Effective masses, bulk gaps and dielectric constants for CdSe, CdS and InP, and measured size-to-emission data.
candidates.pitfall: The color is not a different chemical or a dye inside the dot: it is the confinement energy added to the same material's gap, and bigger dots are redder, not bluer.
candidates.why: The 2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots: https://www.bu.edu/nano-bu/?p=5287
candidates.overlapWith: solar-cells: that page uses a bulk band gap; this one shows the gap itself depending on size once the crystal is nanometres wide.
candidates.needsSource: Material parameters from the literature; size-to-wavelength calibration from Yu, Qu, Guo & Peng, Chem. Mater. 2003 (published numbers, no licensed dataset).

candidates.title: Chromatography: separating by stickiness
candidates.interaction: Inject a mixture at the top of a column and watch each molecule hop at random between the moving phase and the stationary phase, with the time spent stuck set by its partition coefficient, so the bands separate and broaden; a detector at the end draws the chromatogram. Slide the flow rate and the plate height traces the van Deemter curve with its minimum, as eddy paths, diffusion along the column and slow exchange each take their turn at blurring the bands; lengthen the column or change the packing to improve the resolution.
candidates.takeaway: A column separates molecules by how much of the time each spends stuck rather than moving, and there is a best flow speed: slower and diffusion blurs the bands, faster and the molecules cannot keep up with the exchange.
candidates.pitfall: Most chromatography is not a sieve by size: two molecules of the same size separate by how differently they stick, and the bands are Gaussian because the hopping is random.
candidates.why: Undergraduate analytical chemistry teaches band broadening through the van Deemter equation (Bates College chromatography learning objectives): https://www.bates.edu/chemistry-biochemistry/files/2012/01/wenzel-chrom-learning-objectives.pdf
candidates.overlapWith: central-limit-theorem: that page shows why sums of random steps are Gaussian; this one uses that fact to separate molecules and to find the flow rate that separates them best.

candidates.title: Mass spectrometry
candidates.interaction: Ionize a sample and send the ions down a quadrupole whose radio-frequency and DC voltages the reader sets; the page integrates each ion's equation of motion and shows which masses ride stably to the detector and which crash into the rods, with the stability diagram beside. Scan the voltages to sweep across masses and build the spectrum; pick an element or a small molecule and its isotope pattern (chlorine's 3:1 pair, bromine's 1:1 pair) is computed from natural abundances and set beside a measured spectrum.
candidates.takeaway: A mass spectrometer sorts ions by mass-to-charge with electric fields, and only ions within a narrow window of mass ride the oscillating field stably, so sweeping the field reads out the sample one mass at a time.
candidates.needs: Isotopic abundances of the elements and a few reference spectra.
candidates.pitfall: The axis is mass-to-charge, not mass: a doubly charged ion appears at half its mass, and the tallest peak is not necessarily the molecular ion.
candidates.why: OCR A-level Chemistry A (H432) and AQA include mass spectrometry and isotope patterns: https://www.savemyexams.com/learning-hub/exam-specifications/a-level/chemistry/ocr/
candidates.overlapWith: atoms-periodic-table: that page shows isotopes as neutron counts; this one measures them and shows how the instrument does it.
candidates.needsSource: IUPAC/CIAAW isotopic abundances (freely available); MassBank of North America spectra (CC BY 4.0) for comparison.

candidates.title: Dislocations: why metals bend and alloys resist
candidates.interaction: Shear a two-dimensional crystal of simulated atoms with an edge dislocation inside it and watch the defect glide one row of bonds at a time at a stress far below what sliding the whole plane would take; remove the dislocation and the perfect crystal holds until it fails all at once. Sprinkle in larger or smaller foreign atoms and the dislocation snags on them so the crystal needs more stress to yield; keep deforming and dislocations pile up and the metal hardens.
candidates.takeaway: A metal bends at a stress a thousand times below the strength of its bonds because a dislocation moves one row of bonds at a time, and an alloy is harder because foreign atoms get in its way.
candidates.pitfall: Crystals do not deform by whole planes sliding at once; the theoretical strength computed that way is a thousand times higher than what any real metal shows.
candidates.why: MITx 3.012S.3x Structure of Materials covers dislocation descriptors and motion: https://openlearninglibrary.mit.edu/courses/course-v1:MITx+3.012S.3x+1T2019/about
candidates.overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page colors members by stress; this one goes inside the metal to the defect that lets it yield and the atoms that stop it.

candidates.title: Cracks & fracture
candidates.interaction: Stretch a sheet made of a lattice of breakable springs and watch the stress concentrate at the tip of a notch the reader cuts; raise the load until the crack runs, and plot the breaking stress against the notch length to find Griffith's rule. Switch the material from glass-like to metal-like: springs that yield before breaking blunt the tip and absorb energy, so the same crack needs far more stress to run.
candidates.takeaway: A crack grows when the elastic energy it releases pays for the new surface it makes, so a longer crack needs less stress to run, and a material's strength is set by its flaws as much as by its bonds.
candidates.needs: Fracture toughness and modulus values for a few materials, to label the glass-like and metal-like settings.
candidates.pitfall: Strength is not a fixed material constant: Griffith's glass fibres were many times stronger than bulk glass because they had smaller flaws, and a scratch is what makes a pane weak.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 3.22 Mechanical Behavior of Materials covers fracture across metals, ceramics and polymers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-22-mechanical-behavior-of-materials-spring-2008/pages/syllabus
candidates.overlapWith: bridges-structures: that page fails members when their load limit is exceeded; this one shows why the limit depends on cracks and how a crack decides to run.
candidates.needsSource: Published K_IC and modulus values (textbook numbers); the spring network needs no data.

candidates.title: Diffusion in solids

candidates.needs: The diffusion prefactor and activation energy for carbon in iron.
candidates.pitfall: Nothing pushes the atoms toward low concentration; each hops at random, and the net flow from high to low comes only from there being more atoms on one side.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 3.205 covers Fick's laws, self- and interdiffusion and the Kirkendall effect: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-205-thermodynamics-and-kinetics-of-materials-fall-2006/pages/calendar

candidates.title: Nucleation & crystal growth
candidates.interaction: Cool a simulated liquid below its freezing point and watch small clusters form and dissolve until one passes the critical size and grows, while a plot of the free energy of a cluster against its radius shows the hill it had to climb; deepen the undercooling and the hill shrinks, more nuclei survive and the solid ends up as many small grains instead of a few large ones. Then run a phase-field model of a solidifying front on a grid and watch it break into dendrites whose arms thin as the undercooling rises.
candidates.takeaway: A liquid below its freezing point does not freeze at once: a solid seed must first grow past a critical size against its own surface, so deeper undercooling means more seeds and finer grains, and a growing front splits into branches.
candidates.pitfall: Freezing does not start everywhere at once when the freezing point is reached; pure water can be cooled well below 0 °C, and snowflakes branch because the front is unstable, not because the molecules know a shape.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 3.205's calendar runs from diffusion to nucleation, solidification, spinodal decomposition and coarsening: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/3-205-thermodynamics-and-kinetics-of-materials-fall-2006/pages/calendar
candidates.overlapWith: states-of-matter: that page freezes a box at the freezing point; this one shows why it needs a seed, how far it can be undercooled and what shape the solid takes.

candidates.title: Van der Waals forces: why neutral atoms stick

candidates.needs: Polarizabilities and boiling points of the noble gases and halogens.
candidates.pitfall: Dispersion is not negligible: summed over a large molecule it rivals a hydrogen bond and it is the force a gecko climbs with; nor is it a weak form of the chemical bond.

candidates.title: Soap: surfactants & micelles

candidates.title: Noise in gene expression
candidates.interaction: Run a single gene with the Gillespie algorithm: the promoter flicks on and off, each on-period fires a burst of mRNAs, each mRNA a burst of proteins. Set the switching, transcription, translation and decay rates and watch the protein count jitter in one cell while a histogram across a thousand cells widens or narrows. Add a second identical reporter to the same cell and plot one against the other: scatter along the diagonal is shared, extrinsic noise; scatter across it is the gene's own, intrinsic noise.
candidates.takeaway: Genetically identical cells in the same environment differ because their molecules are counted in tens and made in bursts, and a two-reporter scatter plot separates the randomness of the gene itself from the randomness of the cell around it.
candidates.pitfall: Noise does not simply average out at higher expression: bursty expression keeps the Fano factor above one, so the model must produce bursts, not a Poisson stream of single proteins.

candidates.title: Enzyme kinetics: Michaelis-Menten & inhibition
candidates.interaction: Drag the substrate concentration and watch enzyme particles in a box bind, convert and release; the rate climbs and then flattens as every active site is busy, tracing the Michaelis-Menten curve beside the box with Km and Vmax marked. Add a competitive, uncompetitive or mixed inhibitor and see how each bends the curve and its Lineweaver-Burk line; switch to a cooperative enzyme and watch the curve turn sigmoid.
candidates.takeaway: An enzyme's rate saturates because there are only so many active sites, and the shape of that saturation curve, and how an inhibitor changes it, reveals how the enzyme works.
candidates.pitfall: Km is the enzyme's affinity only in the special case where catalysis is much slower than unbinding; the page must show it as a ratio of rate constants (Briggs-Haldane), and Vmax as set by the amount of enzyme, not by the substrate.

candidates.overlapWith: reaction-rates-equilibrium: that page shows collisions crossing a barrier; here the catalyst is a countable set of sites, which produces saturation and inhibition kinetics that uncatalysed collisions do not.

candidates.title: Cell signalling: cascades & ultrasensitivity

Change the phosphatase levels, remove the second phosphorylation site, or close a feedback loop and watch the response steepen, flatten or become bistable; a sketch places the cascade between a receptor and the nucleus.

candidates.overlapWith: the-cell: that page zooms into one cell; this one shows how thousands of cells in a row find out which part of the body they are making.

candidates.title: Turing patterns
candidates.interaction: Run an activator-inhibitor reaction-diffusion system on a grid from near-uniform noise and watch spots or stripes crystallise. Change the ratio of the two diffusion rates and the pattern appears only once the inhibitor spreads much faster than the activator; change the reaction rates to move from spots to stripes to labyrinths; grow the domain and extra stripes insert themselves, and taper the grid into a tail to see spots become bands as it narrows.
candidates.takeaway: Two chemicals, one that makes more of itself and a faster-spreading one that suppresses it, can turn a uniform field into regular spots or stripes with no blueprint, at a wavelength set by rates alone.
candidates.pitfall: Not every stripe in nature is a Turing pattern; the page should name where the mechanism is supported (digits, hair follicles, fish skin) and must not claim it for zebra stripes or fingerprints without saying that is contested.
candidates.why: University of Manchester undergraduate brochure feature on the Turing pattern: https://www.scieng.manchester.ac.uk/undergraduate-brochures/2024/the-turing-pattern/
candidates.overlapWith: chaos-fractals: that page grows patterns by iterating a map; here they grow from a PDE with a definite wavelength, and the control is the diffusion ratio.

candidates.title: The segmentation clock
candidates.interaction: Run a strip of cells along a growing embryo axis, each with a delayed negative-feedback oscillator (the her1/her7 model) and a wavefront that sweeps back as the tail grows and freezes each cell's phase when it passes. Watch waves of expression sweep forward and somites pinch off one per cycle; speed the clock or the wavefront and measure how somite size changes, then couple neighbouring oscillators through Notch and remove the coupling to see the stripes blur.
candidates.takeaway: A body's segments are counted out by a clock: every cycle of an oscillator, a moving front freezes one more block of cells, so segment size equals clock period times front speed.
candidates.pitfall: Somite size is not set by a prepattern of fixed stripes; the page must show that changing the clock period changes the size, which a prepattern could not.
candidates.why: Teaching material rather than a syllabus: tutorial review 'Waves, patterns and bifurcations' on the vertebrate segmentation clock, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.00457 (no curriculum signal found in this round).
candidates.overlapWith: turing-patterns: both make periodic stripes, but here the period is in time and is converted into space by a moving front, with a different model (Lewis 2003 delay oscillator) and a different control.

candidates.title: Central pattern generators
candidates.interaction: Connect two neuron models with mutual inhibition and give them a steady, unpatterned drive; they fall into alternating bursts, the half-centre oscillator. Change the drive to speed the rhythm, swap the burst-ending mechanism (adaptation versus post-inhibitory rebound), then chain twenty such pairs along a lamprey's spine with asymmetric coupling: a wave of contraction travels down the body and the fish swims; reverse the coupling bias and it swims backward.
candidates.takeaway: Rhythmic movement does not need a rhythmic command: two cells that inhibit each other turn a constant signal into alternation, and a chain of them makes a travelling wave.
candidates.pitfall: The half-centre model is a model: lamprey experiments show left-right phasing can survive midline lesions, so the page must present it as the classic mechanism, not the settled one.
candidates.why: Model repository rather than a syllabus: lamprey swimming CPG reference implementation in the Nengo model zoo, https://zoo.nengo.ai/submissions/lamprey/index.html (no curriculum signal found in this round).
candidates.overlapWith: neurons: that page fires one neuron and sums inputs on the next; this one wires neurons into a circuit whose output is a rhythm none of them has alone.

candidates.title: Synaptic plasticity: Hebbian learning & STDP
candidates.interaction: Pair a presynaptic and a postsynaptic spike at a chosen interval and watch the synapse's weight grow when the input leads by a few milliseconds and shrink when it lags, tracing the STDP window over sixty pairings. Then feed a neuron twenty inputs with different timings and let STDP run: the earliest reliable inputs win, the rest fade, and a pattern hidden in noise is picked out. Switch to a plain Hebbian rule without timing and watch the weights run away until a normalisation is added.
candidates.takeaway: Synapses strengthen when the input helps cause the output and weaken when it arrives too late, so a neuron learns to respond to the earliest predictors of its own firing, with no teacher.
candidates.needs: STDP window shape and time constants from Bi & Poo 1998 (published values; the page uses the standard exponential rule, no dataset shipped).
candidates.pitfall: 'Cells that fire together wire together' is incomplete: order matters, and a rule with no depression or no bound makes every weight grow without limit; the page must show the depression side and the need for normalisation.
candidates.why: HSE course 'Mathematical Models of Brain Neural Networks' listing Hodgkin-Huxley, synaptic plasticity and STDP: https://www.hse.ru/edu/courses/835249132
candidates.overlapWith: neural-networks: that page adjusts weights by gradient descent against a target; here the weights change by a local rule from spike timing alone, with no error signal.

candidates.title: Population genetics: drift & selection
candidates.interaction: Run a hundred Wright-Fisher populations at once as allele-frequency traces: with no selection they wander and fix at random, faster in small populations; with a selection coefficient s they bend toward fixation, and a counter shows how often a new beneficial mutation is lost anyway, approaching Kimura's 2s. Set dominance to see recessive alleles hide from selection, and compare the Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies with the simulated ones each generation.
candidates.takeaway: Allele frequencies change by chance as well as by selection, and in a small population chance wins: most beneficial mutations are lost before selection can act on them.
candidates.pitfall: Hardy-Weinberg is not 'evolution stops': it is the one-generation baseline that shows which forces are absent, and drift is not selection by another name; the page must keep them separate.
candidates.why: Cal State LA BIOL 415 Population Genetics syllabus (Hardy-Weinberg, drift, effective size, selection, coalescent): https://www.calstatela.edu/sites/default/files/syllabibiol415.pdf
candidates.overlapWith: evolution: that page shifts a trait distribution with predators and food; this one tracks a single allele's frequency and separates chance from selection with explicit N and s.

candidates.title: The coalescent
candidates.interaction: Sample ten gene copies from a population and step backwards one generation at a time: each copy picks a parent at random, two lineages that pick the same parent merge, and the genealogy grows down to a single ancestor with its branch lengths. Rerun to see how much the tree varies, change the population size and watch the time to the common ancestor scale with it, and sprinkle mutations on the branches to produce the sample's sequence differences. Squeeze the population through a bottleneck and see the genealogy and the diversity collapse.
candidates.takeaway: The pattern of differences in a sample of DNA sequences is the shadow of a random genealogy, and reading that genealogy backwards tells you how large the population was and when it shrank.
candidates.pitfall: The most recent common ancestor of a sample is not the first human or a single couple; different genes have different ancestors at different times, and the page should show two loci with different trees.
candidates.why: coalesceR, a pedagogical R package for teaching the basics of coalescent theory: https://rdrr.io/rforge/coalesceR
candidates.overlapWith: population-genetics: that page runs time forward for a whole population; this one runs it backward for a sample, which is how real sequence data are read.

candidates.title: Phylogenetics: building the tree of life
candidates.interaction: Pick a handful of species, align their cytochrome b sequences and watch the page count differences into a distance matrix. Build the tree by UPGMA, merging the closest pair step by step, then rebuild it by neighbour joining and see where the two disagree; speed up one lineage's clock and watch UPGMA put it in the wrong place; switch to a parsimony score and drag branches to try to beat the algorithm.
candidates.takeaway: A tree of life is not observed but computed from the differences between sequences, and a method's assumptions, such as a constant rate of change, decide which tree it finds.
candidates.needs: Mitochondrial cytochrome b (or 16S rRNA) sequences for a dozen species from GenBank (NCBI places no restrictions on reuse); the species' accepted relationships from the Open Tree of Life synthetic tree for comparison (reported CC0, to confirm on the project site).
candidates.pitfall: Humans are not at the 'top' of the tree and no living species is the ancestor of another: the page must let the reader rotate nodes to show that only the branching order carries information.
candidates.why: CUHK BMEG3102 Bioinformatics tutorial on molecular phylogenetics (UPGMA, NJ, parsimony, likelihood): https://webarchive.lib.cuhk.edu.hk/20210407143348mp_/http:/www.cse.cuhk.edu.hk/~qdou/bmeg3102/tutorials/BMEG3102_2021Spring_Tutorial06_MolecularPhylogenetics_CUHK.pdf
candidates.overlapWith: deep-time: that page scrubs a dated timeline of life; this one computes the branching order from today's sequences and has no dates until a clock is assumed.
candidates.needsSource: GenBank sequences, no reuse restrictions (load-bearing); Open Tree of Life reported CC0, to confirm.

candidates.title: Speciation
candidates.interaction: Split a population in two with a barrier and let each half accumulate its own mutations in a set of interacting genes, each change neutral or useful at home. Lift the barrier after a chosen time and cross the two: hybrid fitness falls as pairs of alleles that never met prove incompatible (Dobzhansky-Muller), and a counter shows incompatibilities growing faster than linearly with time. Let gene flow leak through the barrier to see divergence stall, and add selection against hybrids to watch reinforcement finish the job.
candidates.takeaway: Two populations become species not by one changing into something new but by each drifting along its own path until their genes no longer work together, and the barrier between them grows faster the longer they are apart.
candidates.pitfall: No single mutation makes a new species and no individual is 'the first' of one; incompatibilities arise between alleles that were each harmless where they evolved.
candidates.why: MERLOT peer-reviewed classroom activity modelling the Dobzhansky-Muller process: https://awscbdev.merlot.org/merlot/viewMaterial.htm?id=851638
candidates.overlapWith: evolution: that page adapts one population to its environment; this one follows two separated populations and measures the barrier that grows between them.

candidates.title: Evolutionary game theory
candidates.interaction: Set the payoffs of a hawk-dove contest and release a population of players; replicator dynamics pulls the share of hawks to the mixed equilibrium that neither strategy can invade, drawn as a flow on a line. Switch to the prisoner's dilemma and watch cooperators die out, then place the players on a grid where they meet neighbours and see clusters of cooperators survive; add relatedness between players and find the cost-to-benefit ratio at which helping kin pays, Hamilton's rule.
candidates.takeaway: When fitness depends on what others do, the winning strategy is the one that cannot be invaded rather than the one that scores most, and cooperation survives only when cooperators meet each other more often than chance.
candidates.pitfall: Evolutionary stability does not mean the population is at its best: hawks persist even though a population of doves would score higher, and the page must show that the equilibrium is not the optimum.
candidates.why: ELTE course on evolutionary game theory (hawk-dove, replicator dynamics, ESS, altruism): https://neptun.elte.hu/MobilityCourses/Course/evojatsb22em
candidates.overlapWith: evolution: that page's fitness is fixed by the environment; here fitness depends on what the rest of the population does, which produces equilibria that selection on a fixed landscape never does. It also covers the biological half of the Reserve item 'Game theory' (replicator dynamics, ESS), leaving classical game theory to a math lens.

candidates.title: Origin of life & the error threshold
candidates.interaction: Run a pool of self-copying RNA strings on a fitness peak with a chosen copying error rate per base and a chosen length: below a threshold the population clusters around the best sequence as a cloud of mutants, above it the information melts into random sequences. Lengthen the genome and watch the threshold fall, then let the strings evolve a copying enzyme with better fidelity and see the longest sustainable genome grow; close with parasites exploiting a shared replicase and compartments containing them.
candidates.takeaway: A replicator can carry only as much information as its copying accuracy allows, so the first genomes had to be short, and getting longer required evolving better copiers first.
candidates.pitfall: The error threshold has no single agreed definition and the RNA world is a hypothesis; the page must not present the simulation as a reconstruction of how life began.
candidates.why: Wikipedia, 'Error threshold (evolution)' (Eigen's paradox and the RNA world): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_threshold_(evolution)
candidates.overlapWith: error-correction: that page adds redundancy to a message to survive noise; here the message is a genome that must copy itself through noise, and the question is how long it can be.

candidates.title: Luria-Delbruck: mutations before selection
candidates.interaction: Step through the 1943 experiment: grow twenty cultures from single cells for a chosen number of generations at a chosen mutation rate, plate them all on a phage lawn, and count the survivors. If mutations arose only on contact with the phage the counts would be Poisson and nearly equal; instead a few plates hold hundreds of mutants, the jackpots, because a mutation that happened early was inherited by a whole clone. Replay with mutations induced at plating to see the Poisson alternative, and estimate the mutation rate from the fraction of empty plates.
candidates.takeaway: Mutations happen before and regardless of the challenge they will later face, and the wild spread between replicate cultures is the signature of that.
candidates.pitfall: The jackpot distribution does not show that the environment induces mutations; it shows the opposite, and the page must make the Poisson alternative explicit so the reader sees it fail.
candidates.why: 'Fascination with Fluctuation: Luria and Delbruck's Legacy', on the experiment in undergraduate mathematics education (University of Delaware): https://udspace.udel.edu/items/2837763f-b87a-465a-9701-2b96405d98f5/full
candidates.overlapWith: evolution: that page's pitfall says mutations do not arise because they are needed; this one is the experiment that proved it, run as a statistics-of-clones simulation.

candidates.title: The microbiome as an ecosystem
candidates.interaction: Run a gut community of ten bacterial groups with the interaction matrix Stein et al. inferred from mouse data; it settles to a stable mix. Dose it with an antibiotic for a chosen number of days and watch some groups crash and others bloom; introduce C. difficile before, during and after the course and see it fail, invade, or take hold; stop the antibiotic and find that the community does not always return, then transplant a healthy community to push it back.
candidates.takeaway: A gut community is a web of competition and support with more than one stable state, so a disturbance can tip it into a new one that persists after the disturbance is gone.
candidates.needs: Generalized Lotka-Volterra interaction matrix and antibiotic susceptibilities from Stein et al. 2013, PLOS Computational Biology (CC BY).
candidates.pitfall: The parameters come from mice and one antibiotic, and gLV fits are uncertain; the page must say the model illustrates the dynamics and is not a prediction for a human gut.
candidates.why: Demand: public coverage of ecological modelling of the gut microbiota (Gut Microbiota for Health): https://www.gutmicrobiotaforhealth.com/ecological-modeling-of-intestinal-microbiota/ ; model source is Stein et al. 2013, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1003388 (no curriculum signal found in this round).
candidates.overlapWith: ecosystems: that page has one predator, one prey and a small food web; here a ten-group community with alternative stable states, driven by real inferred interactions and perturbed by an antibiotic.
candidates.needsSource: PLOS Computational Biology article and supplementary parameters, CC BY.

candidates.title: Rubisco, photorespiration & C4 plants
candidates.interaction: Run the Farquhar-von Caemmerer-Berry model of a leaf: set CO2, oxygen, light and temperature and watch Rubisco split its time between fixing CO2 and wastefully grabbing O2, with the assimilation curve against CO2 drawn live and the limiting step marked. Raise the temperature and watch photorespiration eat the gain; then switch the leaf to a C4 anatomy that pumps CO2 into the bundle sheath, or to CAM that opens its stomata at night, and compare carbon gain and water loss across a hot day.
candidates.takeaway: The enzyme at the base of nearly all food confuses oxygen with CO2, and C4 and CAM plants are two engineering fixes that concentrate CO2 around it or move its work to the night.
candidates.needs: Rubisco kinetic constants and their temperature dependence (von Caemmerer 2000; Bernacchi et al. 2001; published values).
candidates.pitfall: C4 is not 'better' photosynthesis: at cool temperatures and low light its extra ATP cost makes it lose to C3, and the page must show the crossover.
candidates.why: POGIL classroom activity 'C4 and CAM Photosynthesis' for upper-level plant physiology: https://pac.pogil.org/index.php/pac/article/view/557
candidates.overlapWith: photosynthesis: that page follows photons to sugar in one chloroplast; this one is the enzyme kinetics of the carbon-fixing step and the leaf-level consequences of its oxygen mistake.

candidates.title: Metabolic networks & flux balance
candidates.interaction: Open a map of central carbon metabolism (glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, the TCA cycle, fermentation, respiration) with every reaction's stoichiometry, and choose what the cell maximises and what it may take up. A linear-programme solver in the browser finds the flux through every reaction, drawn as arrow widths; cut the oxygen supply and watch flux reroute to fermentation, knock out a gene and see whether growth survives by a detour, and sweep the glucose uptake to trace growth rate against it.
candidates.takeaway: Knowing only which reactions exist and that nothing accumulates, a cell's best possible division of flux can be computed, and the network's detours are what make most single knockouts survivable.
candidates.needs: A documented core E. coli network. The BiGG e_coli_core model is free for educational and non-profit use but not openly licensed (UC Regents terms), so build the network from textbook stoichiometry with references, or from a CC0 BioModels-curated central-metabolism model.
candidates.pitfall: FBA predicts a bound, not a measurement: it has no kinetics and no regulation, so the page must say that the optimum is a hypothesis about what the cell maximises and that real fluxes can differ.
candidates.why: UCSD Systems Biology Research Group FBA tutorial with the core E. coli model: https://sbrg.ucsd.edu/node/61
candidates.overlapWith: respiration-atp: that page follows one glucose through the pathways; this one treats the whole network at once and asks how flux divides among all routes.
candidates.needsSource: BiGG e_coli_core is non-commercial only (weak); textbook stoichiometry needs no licence; BioModels is CC0.

candidates.title: Viral replication inside a host
candidates.interaction: Infect a host in the Perelson model: virus enters target cells, infected cells bud new virions and die, and viral load climbs to a plateau where production and clearance balance. Start a drug that blocks new infections and watch the load fall in two phases whose slopes give the half-lives of free virus (hours) and of infected cells (about a day); stop the drug early and it rebounds; let the virus mutate at a chosen rate and see a resistant strain take over under one drug but not under three.
candidates.takeaway: A steady viral load is not a quiet infection but a furious balance of billions of virions made and cleared every day, which is why resistance evolves so fast and why combination therapy works.
candidates.pitfall: The two-phase decay and its half-lives are estimates fitted to patients by Perelson et al.; the page must present them as fitted values, not as constants of the virus.
candidates.why: q-bio Summer School 'Viral Dynamics' (Perelson's lecture 'How to model a viral infection within the host'): https://q-bio.org/wiki/The_Seventh_q-bio_Summer_School:_Viral_Dynamics
candidates.overlapWith: epidemics: that page counts infected people; this one counts infected cells inside one person, where the same kind of equations give half-lives rather than reproduction numbers.

candidates.title: Caches & the memory hierarchy
candidates.interaction: Choose a program's access pattern (sum an array row by row or column by column, walk a linked list, multiply matrices with and without blocking) and run it through a cache with adjustable size, line length, associativity and replacement policy; each access lights a line as a hit or a miss, and the miss count and the average memory access time plot live. Add a second level of cache and watch where the knee of the curve moves.
candidates.takeaway: The same program runs many times faster or slower depending only on whether it touches memory in an order the cache can predict.
candidates.pitfall: A bigger cache is not always better: a direct-mapped cache thrashes on a stride equal to its size however large it is, and the unit moved is a whole line, never a byte, so a miss costs the same for one byte as for sixty-four.
candidates.why: MIT 6.004 Computation Structures, Unit 14 'Multilevel memories: locality, performance, caches' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/calendar
candidates.overlapWith: cpu: that page single-steps instructions against a flat memory that answers instantly; this page makes memory itself the model and shows why one access costs one cycle and the next two hundred.

candidates.title: Virtual memory & paging
candidates.interaction: Pan across the address spaces of two processes that both use address 0x1000 and follow any address through its page table to a physical frame, with the TLB holding the recent translations and a hover showing each step. Run the processes until they ask for more memory than the machine has, watch pages fault in and get evicted to disk, and compare FIFO, LRU and the clock algorithm on the same reference string, including the case where adding frames causes more faults.
candidates.takeaway: Every program sees its own private, contiguous memory, but that memory is an illusion assembled page by page from wherever free frames and disk happen to be.
candidates.pitfall: Swapping is not what makes the memory 'virtual': isolation and relocation are the point, and a machine with no swap still uses it. A page fault is normal operation, not an error.
candidates.why: MIT 6.004 Computation Structures, L18 'Virtual memory: mapping, protection, contexts' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/calendar (also Berkeley CS162 Fall 2023, three Virtual Memory lectures)
candidates.overlapWith: cpu: that page addresses a single flat memory directly; this page puts a translation between every address and the frame that holds it, so many programs can share and be protected from each other.

candidates.title: Pipelines & branch prediction
candidates.interaction: Feed a short program into a five-stage pipeline and step it cycle by cycle while instructions overlap in a pipeline diagram; a dependency between neighbouring instructions stalls the pipe until forwarding is switched on. Insert a loop and compare a predictor that always guesses 'not taken' with a two-bit counter, counting the cycles thrown away on each misprediction, then deepen the pipeline and watch that cost grow.
candidates.takeaway: A pipelined processor finishes an instruction nearly every cycle only while it can guess what comes next; each wrong guess empties the pipe.
candidates.pitfall: Pipelining does not make any single instruction faster; it raises throughput, and a deeper pipeline raises the price of every hazard.
candidates.why: MIT 6.004 Computation Structures, Unit 15 'Pipelining the Beta: pipeline diagrams, data hazards' and 'control hazards and exceptions' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-004-computation-structures-spring-2017/pages/calendar
candidates.overlapWith: cpu: that page runs one instruction at a time through fetch, decode and execute; this page overlaps several in flight and shows what breaks when they depend on each other.

candidates.title: Operating systems: processes & scheduling
candidates.interaction: Create a handful of jobs with different lengths and I/O habits and run them on one core under first-come-first-served, shortest-job-first, round robin with an adjustable time slice and a multi-level feedback queue; a Gantt chart fills in and each job's turnaround and response time are plotted. Add a context-switch cost and a second core and watch the fair policies lose throughput and an interactive job go unresponsive under the wrong one.
candidates.takeaway: A single processor appears to run many programs at once by switching between them many times a second, and which one it picks next decides whether the machine feels fast or fair.
candidates.pitfall: Shortest-job-first minimises average turnaround but the scheduler cannot know job lengths in advance; the feedback queue's whole point is that it learns them from how each job behaves.
candidates.why: Berkeley CS162 Operating Systems and Systems Programming, scheduling lectures (course description: 'resource allocation and scheduling') https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs162/fa23
candidates.overlapWith: cpu: that page runs a single program; this page is what runs on top of it to share one processor between many.

candidates.title: Locks, races & deadlock
candidates.interaction: Drag the interleaving of two threads that both increment a shared counter and watch the final value come out wrong; add a lock and the bad interleavings disappear. Then seat philosophers around a table, assign each an order for picking up forks and run them until they freeze, with a resource-allocation graph that shows the cycle; break it by ordering the locks or by a timeout and compare.
candidates.takeaway: Two correct programs sharing memory can produce a wrong answer, and the locks that fix it can freeze both forever unless they are always taken in the same order.
candidates.pitfall: A data race is not a rare glitch: an unsynchronised increment loses updates under every scheduler. Deadlock needs all four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait), so removing any one of them prevents it.
candidates.why: Berkeley CS162, 'Synchronization (Finish), Scheduling' lecture https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs162/fa16 (the free OSTEP textbook's 'Common Concurrency Problems' chapter covers the same ground)
candidates.overlapWith: consensus-blockchains: that page gets machines to agree over a network; this one is agreement between threads inside one machine that share memory, where the failure is silent corruption or a freeze.

candidates.title: Compilers
candidates.interaction: Type a small program in a toy language and step it through the compiler: characters become tokens, tokens a parse tree, the tree an intermediate form, and the intermediate form instructions for the minimal processor of the CPU page, which then runs them. Toggle optimisations (constant folding, dead-code elimination, register allocation by graph colouring) and watch the emitted code shrink and the instruction count fall; introduce a syntax error and see exactly where the parser gives up.
candidates.takeaway: A compiler is a chain of mechanical translations, each simple on its own, that turns text a person wrote into instructions a processor can run.
candidates.pitfall: A compiler does not understand the program: parsing is a grammar check, and an optimisation may change the code only where it can prove the result is unchanged, which is why it often cannot.
candidates.why: Stanford CS143 Compilers (lexical analysis, parsing, code generation, register allocation) https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs143/
candidates.overlapWith: cpu: that page runs hand-written assembly; this page shows where the assembly comes from and reuses the same processor so the output actually runs.

candidates.title: Garbage collection
candidates.interaction: Run a small program that allocates objects and drops references, shown as a heap of boxes with pointers; press collect and watch mark-and-sweep trace from the roots and free what it never reached, then switch to a copying collector that compacts the survivors and to a generational one that collects only the nursery most of the time. Tune the heap size and watch pause length and memory use trade against each other; build a cycle of objects and see reference counting leak it.
candidates.takeaway: A collector never knows what the program will need; it keeps whatever is still reachable from the running program and reclaims everything else.
candidates.pitfall: Reference counting is not the whole story: it cannot free cycles, and 'the program is done with this object' is undecidable in general, so reachability is the proxy every collector uses.
candidates.why: UC Berkeley CS61B, Lecture 39 'Garbage collection' (mark-sweep, copying, generational) https://inst.eecs.berkeley.edu/~cs61b/fa17/materials/lectures/lect39.pdf
candidates.overlapWith: graph-search: marking is a graph traversal; graph-search finds a path, this page uses the traversal to decide what memory can be thrown away and shows the pauses it costs.

candidates.title: Hash tables & Bloom filters
candidates.interaction: Insert keys into a table with chaining or open addressing and raise the load factor; every probe is drawn, and the measured mean probe length is plotted against the expected curve until the table resizes and rehashes. Then feed the same keys to a Bloom filter with an adjustable bit array and number of hash functions, query keys that were never inserted and watch the measured false-positive rate track the formula; degrade the hash function with a slider and see both structures cluster.
candidates.takeaway: A good hash spreads keys evenly, so lookups stay constant-time until the table fills, and a Bloom filter trades a known, tunable false-positive rate for a fraction of the memory.
candidates.pitfall: A hash table's constant time is an average under a good hash, not a guarantee; the cryptographic hash of the cryptography page is a different tool; and a Bloom filter can only ever say 'definitely absent', never 'definitely present'.
candidates.why: MIT 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms, Lecture 4 'Hashing' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/pages/lecture-notes (Bloom filters appear in CMU 15-445's index lectures)
candidates.overlapWith: cryptography: that page shows a hash as a one-way fingerprint; here the hash is a fast bucket index, and the model is the statistics of collisions as the table fills.

candidates.title: Databases: B-trees & transactions
candidates.interaction: Insert and delete keys in a B+tree of adjustable fan-out and watch nodes split and merge, with the disk reads per lookup counted and compared with a binary tree on the same keys. Then run two transactions that interleave on the same rows with a write-ahead log, crash the machine at any point and replay the log to recover, and compare locking with snapshot isolation on an update that each transaction alone would get right.
candidates.takeaway: A database keeps rows findable in a handful of disk reads by keeping its tree short and wide, and keeps them correct through a crash by writing its intentions down before acting on them.
candidates.pitfall: 'Atomic' means all-or-nothing, not instantaneous, and a transaction is durable once its log record reaches disk, not when the rows are updated; the data pages can be stale at a crash and still be recovered.
candidates.why: CMU 15-445 Database Systems, Lecture 08 'B+Tree Index' https://15445.courses.cs.cmu.edu/spring2024/slides/08-trees.pdf
candidates.overlapWith: consensus-blockchains: that page replicates one log among machines; this one is a single machine's log and index, and why a tree rather than a chain is what makes lookup fast.

candidates.title: P vs NP & SAT solving
candidates.interaction: Build a puzzle (colour a small map, or seat guests under constraints) and watch it compile into clauses; run a solver that propagates forced choices, branches, and learns a new clause from each conflict, with the search tree drawn as it is pruned. Generate random 3-SAT and sweep the clause-to-variable ratio: the solver's effort spikes near 4.26, where the formulas switch from almost always satisfiable to almost never.
candidates.takeaway: A solver that learns from its dead ends prunes the search far below brute force, and random formulas turn hardest exactly where they switch from almost always satisfiable to almost never.
candidates.pitfall: NP does not mean 'exponential'; it means a solution can be checked quickly. NP-complete problems are solved routinely in practice, just not with a worst-case guarantee, and a quantum computer is not known to change that.
candidates.why: MIT 6.045J Automata, Computability and Complexity, Lecture 15 'Polynomial-time reducibility, NP-completeness, SAT' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-045j-automata-computability-and-complexity-spring-2011/resources/mit6_045js11_lec15

candidates.title: Regular expressions & automata
candidates.interaction: Type a regular expression and watch it become a Thompson NFA, then collapse into a DFA by subset construction; feed it text one character at a time and watch the set of active states move. Race the DFA against a backtracking matcher on a pattern such as (a?)^n a^n: one runs in time linear in the input while the other explodes. Try to write a pattern for balanced parentheses and see the pumping argument show why no finite machine can.
candidates.takeaway: A regular expression is a finite machine in disguise, which is why it can match in a single pass; what no finite machine can count, no regular expression can match.
candidates.pitfall: Modern 'regex' engines with backreferences are not regular, and the exponential blow-up (ReDoS) is a property of the backtracking implementation, not of the language being matched.
candidates.why: Russ Cox, 'Regular Expression Matching Can Be Simple And Fast' (Thompson NFA, 20 microseconds against Perl's 60 seconds) https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp1.html
candidates.overlapWith: turing-machines: Turing machines are the top of the hierarchy; this page is its bottom, a machine with no tape, and shows exactly what that costs and what it buys.

candidates.title: Floating point
candidates.interaction: Zoom along the number line and watch the representable numbers thin out away from zero, with the bits of the selected value shown; type 0.1 + 0.2 and see where each operand lands and why the sum misses 0.3 by one unit in the last place. Subtract two nearly equal numbers and watch the significant digits vanish, sum a million small numbers in two orders and compare, then switch on compensated summation; run the same calculation in half, single and double precision.
candidates.takeaway: A floating-point number is the nearest representable value, not the number itself, and the gap between neighbours grows with size, so the order of operations changes the answer.
candidates.pitfall: Floating-point arithmetic is not random or buggy: each operation is correctly rounded and its error is predictable from the exponent; the trouble is accumulation and cancellation, not the single operation.
candidates.why: Computerphile 'Floating Point Numbers', about 2.5 million views (view count from aggregator snapshots found this session; the video id is recalled, not fetched this session) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PZRI1IfStY0
candidates.overlapWith: binary: that page reads one bit pattern as a float; this page explores the gaps between floats and what they do to arithmetic.

candidates.title: Lambda calculus & types
candidates.interaction: Write expressions in a language with three forms (variable, function, application) and step the reductions, with the redex highlighted and the substitution animated; encode numbers and booleans as functions and watch addition happen by substitution alone. Reduce the Y combinator to see recursion appear from nothing, run the self-applying omega and watch it never halt, then switch on simple types and see the same term rejected.
candidates.takeaway: Functions alone, with substitution as the only rule, are enough to compute anything a computer can; adding types removes some programs, and with them the ones that never stop.
candidates.pitfall: It is not just functional-programming notation: evaluation order matters (normal order finds a normal form whenever one exists, applicative order can loop), and the simply typed calculus is not Turing-complete, which is the point of it.
candidates.why: Computerphile 'Lambda Calculus' (Graham Hutton), about 1.08 million views (view count from aggregator snapshots found this session; the video id is recalled, not fetched this session) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eis11j_iGMs

candidates.title: Pseudo-random numbers
candidates.interaction: Pick a generator (a linear congruential generator with editable multiplier and modulus, xorshift, a counter-based one) and a seed, and plot successive outputs as points in two and three dimensions; rotate the cloud until RANDU's points collapse onto fifteen planes. Run a chi-square and a serial test live, shrink the modulus until the period shows as repetition, and reseed from the clock or from real entropy to see when the sequence is reproducible and when it must not be.
candidates.takeaway: A computer's random numbers are a deterministic sequence that merely looks random, and a bad generator hides its pattern until you look at it from the right angle.
candidates.pitfall: Passing statistical tests is not security: a simulation generator can be predicted from a few outputs and must not make keys, and seeding with the time does not make it unpredictable.
candidates.why: Marsaglia, 'Random numbers fall mainly in the planes', PNAS 1968 (RANDU's triples lie on 15 planes) https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC285899
candidates.overlapWith: chaos-fractals: the logistic map there is deterministic chaos; here determinism is engineered to pass as randomness, and the lattice structure is the tell.

candidates.title: The fast Fourier transform
candidates.interaction: Step the recursion on 8, 16 or 64 samples: split even and odd, recurse, and combine with twiddle factors drawn as rotations on the unit circle, in a butterfly diagram that grows with n. Count the multiplications against the direct transform as n doubles, then use the result to multiply two long polynomials (or two big integers) and watch the product appear in n log n steps.
candidates.takeaway: The Fourier transform of n samples takes n squared steps done directly, but the two halves of the problem share nearly all their work, and reusing it brings the cost down to n log n.
candidates.pitfall: The FFT is not an approximation or a different transform: it computes exactly the discrete Fourier transform, only faster, and it needs evenly spaced samples.
candidates.why: MIT 6.046J Design and Analysis of Algorithms, Lecture 3 'Divide & Conquer: FFT' (Demaine: 'probably the most taught algorithm at MIT') https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-046j-design-and-analysis-of-algorithms-spring-2015/resources/lecture-3-divide-conquer-fft/

candidates.title: Dynamic programming
candidates.interaction: Watch the recursion tree for the edit distance between two words explode with repeated subproblems, then fill the table cell by cell and trace the cheapest path back to the alignment.
