candidates.takeaway: When a problem's subproblems overlap, solving each once and looking it up turns an exponential search into a table that fills in polynomial time.
candidates.needs: One CC0 photograph for seam carving (Wikimedia Commons CC0, or a public-domain NASA image).
candidates.pitfall: The name has nothing to do with programming or dynamics: it is memoised recursion, and it only works when an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions of subproblems, which the travelling-salesman problem does not offer in polynomial size.

candidates.title: Cellular automata & universality
candidates.interaction: Sweep through the 256 elementary rules on a one-dimensional strip and sort them by what they do (die out, repeat, grow a fractal, stay chaotic), then switch to Conway's Life and place gliders, blinkers and a glider gun. Guided challenges aim streams of gliders at each other to build a NOT gate and an AND gate from collisions, then wire them into the half adder of the logic-gates page, which is the reason no shortcut can predict Life's future in general.
candidates.takeaway: A rule a child can follow on graph paper can carry signals and compute with them: streams of gliders colliding at the right angle make a working logic gate.
candidates.pitfall: Emergence here is not mysticism: every pattern follows from the rule, and universality is a theorem (Cook 2004 for rule 110, glider logic for Life), not a metaphor. Most rules do nothing interesting; the page must not imply that complexity is the norm.
candidates.why: Wikipedia, 'Conway's Game of Life': 'the best-known example of a cellular automaton', Gardner 1970; the dedicated LifeWiki holds over 2,000 articles https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conway%27s_Game_of_Life

candidates.title: TCP congestion control
candidates.interaction: Send a file across a link with a bottleneck and a queue of adjustable size, and watch the sender's window grow in slow start, collapse on a loss and resume with additive increase, tracing the sawtooth of throughput against time. Add a second flow and see the two converge to a fair share; oversize the buffer and watch delay balloon while throughput does not improve; compare Reno, CUBIC and a delay-based sender on the same link.
candidates.takeaway: The Internet has no traffic police; every sender probes for its share of the bottleneck by speeding up until packets drop and backing off, and that simple rule is what keeps the network from collapsing.
candidates.pitfall: Congestion control is not flow control: the receiver's window protects the receiver, the congestion window protects the network. A loss on a wireless link is often noise rather than congestion, which classic TCP misreads as a signal to slow down.
candidates.why: Stanford CS144 Introduction to Computer Networking, transport unit: 'reliable delivery over an unreliable network, flow control, and congestion control' (AIMD, Tahoe, Reno) https://bulletin.stanford.edu/courses/2075241
candidates.overlapWith: internet: that page shows a lost packet being resent; this page is the rate-control loop that decides how fast to send in the first place, and what happens when every sender runs it at once.

candidates.title: TLS: how a connection becomes private
candidates.interaction: Step through a TLS 1.3 handshake between a browser and a server: hello messages carrying key shares, an elliptic-curve key exchange, a certificate chain checked signature by signature up to a root the browser already trusts, and the derivation of the session keys that then encrypt every record. Put an attacker in the middle who swaps in his own key share: the certificate check fails visibly; later reveal the server's long-term key and see that past sessions stay unreadable.
candidates.takeaway: A padlock means two strangers agreed a fresh secret in the open, and one of them proved who it was through a chain of signatures leading to someone the browser already trusts.
candidates.needs: One real certificate chain, for example the site's own GitHub Pages chain; certificates are public documents.
candidates.pitfall: The padlock says nothing about the site being honest, only that you are talking to the holder of that certificate. Key exchange and authentication are separate jobs: Diffie-Hellman alone is defeated by a man in the middle, which is exactly what the certificate prevents.
candidates.why: Cloudflare Learning Center, 'What happens in a TLS handshake?' https://cloudflare.com/learning/ssl/what-happens-in-a-tls-handshake
candidates.overlapWith: cryptography: that page shows key exchange, hashing and signing separately on small numbers; this page is the protocol that combines them, with the certificate chain as the new piece.

candidates.title: Zero-knowledge proofs
candidates.interaction: Colour a small graph with three colours, cover every vertex, and let the verifier uncover one random edge; repeat with a fresh random permutation of the colours each round and watch a cheater's chance of surviving fall round by round while the verifier's transcript never contains a full colouring. Then run the Schnorr protocol on small numbers: prove you know a discrete logarithm without revealing it, and watch a simulator forge a transcript that nobody could tell from a real one.
candidates.takeaway: You can convince someone that a statement is true while their view of the exchange contains nothing they could not have made up themselves.
candidates.pitfall: Zero-knowledge is a property of what the verifier learns, not a kind of encryption, and a single round proves almost nothing: soundness comes from repetition, and the verifier's choices must be unpredictable.
candidates.why: Computerphile 'Zero Knowledge Proofs', about 235,000 views (view count from aggregator snapshots found this session; the video id is recalled, not fetched this session) https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HUs1bH85X9I
candidates.overlapWith: cryptography: that page proves identity with a signature, which reveals the signed message; this page proves knowledge while revealing nothing, and the probability of a cheater surviving is the graphic.

candidates.title: Elliptic-curve cryptography
candidates.interaction: Drag two points on an elliptic curve over the real numbers and watch the chord-and-tangent rule produce their sum; switch the same curve to a finite field and the smooth curve becomes a scatter of points on which the same rule still works. Multiply a point by k with double-and-add, step by step, and see that landing on a target point gives no clue what k was; then run Diffie-Hellman on the curve and compare the key sizes with the modular version.
candidates.takeaway: Adding points on a curve is easy to do and, over a finite field, practically impossible to undo, so a 256-bit curve key does the job of a 3,000-bit modular one.
candidates.needs: Curve parameters from public standards (secp256k1, Curve25519), which are published specifications.
candidates.pitfall: The picture over the real numbers is for intuition only: the cryptography lives on the finite-field points, where there is no curve to see, and the hardness is the discrete logarithm, not the shape. 'Elliptic' has nothing to do with ellipses.
candidates.why: Cloudflare, 'A (relatively easy to understand) primer on elliptic curve cryptography' https://blog.cloudflare.com/a-relatively-easy-to-understand-primer-on-elliptic-curve-cryptography/
candidates.overlapWith: cryptography: that page does Diffie-Hellman with modular exponentiation on a clock face; this page swaps the group for curve points and shows why that buys so much for so few bits.

candidates.title: Radar & sonar
candidates.interaction: Fire a pulse at targets you place and drag, and watch the echoes return on a range display; shorten the pulse for resolution and lose energy, then replace it with a chirp and a matched filter and get both at once. Set a target moving and read its speed from the Doppler shift, build a range-Doppler map, raise the noise until targets vanish into clutter, and switch the medium to water to see why sonar runs slow and low-frequency.
candidates.takeaway: Radar and sonar measure distance by timing an echo and speed by its pitch, and the shape of the pulse decides how finely each can be told apart.
candidates.pitfall: Range comes from timing, not triangulation; stealth is mostly about where the echo goes, not about absorbing it; and the Doppler shift measures only the speed toward or away from the antenna.
candidates.why: MIT OCW RES.LL-003, 'Build a Small Radar System Capable of Sensing Range, Doppler, and Synthetic Aperture Radar Imaging' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/res-ll-003-build-a-small-radar-system-capable-of-sensing-range-doppler-and-synthetic-aperture-radar-imaging-january-iap-2011/
candidates.overlapWith: medical-imaging: that page reconstructs an image from projections and mentions ultrasound in passing; this page is the echo itself: pulse shape, matched filtering and Doppler.

candidates.title: Antenna arrays, beamforming & MIMO
candidates.interaction: Set the spacing and relative phases of a row of antennas and watch the radiation pattern form a beam; steer it by phase alone, add elements to narrow it and widen the spacing until grating lobes appear. Then place scatterers between a transmitting and a receiving array: the page computes the channel matrix from the path geometry, and its singular values show how many independent streams the link can carry, from one in open line of sight to several in a cluttered room.
candidates.takeaway: Many antennas can aim a signal without moving, and in a cluttered environment can send several signals at once over the same frequencies, which is where modern wireless capacity comes from.
candidates.pitfall: Multipath is not only an enemy: MIMO needs scattering to work, and a clean line of sight gives one stream. A beam is formed by interference between elements, not by any element pointing anywhere.
candidates.why: Stanford EE359 Wireless Communications, MIMO lectures 14 and 15 https://ee359.stanford.edu/pdfs/syllabusWIN20.pdf
candidates.overlapWith: wireless-signals: that page modulates one carrier from one antenna; this page is what many antennas add, direction and parallel streams.

candidates.title: The Kalman filter
candidates.interaction: Track a moving object from a noisy sensor: at each step the filter predicts where the object will be, then blends in the new measurement, with the estimate's uncertainty drawn as an ellipse that grows on prediction and shrinks on measurement. Turn the measurement noise up and watch the filter lean on its model; add a second sensor (an accelerometer to the GPS fix) and see the fused estimate beat either alone; make the object swerve and watch a filter with the wrong motion model lag behind, confidently.
candidates.takeaway: The best estimate of where something is comes from weighing a prediction against a measurement in proportion to how much each can be trusted, and the filter keeps that weighting up to date.
candidates.pitfall: It does not average measurements: with a good model it can be more certain than any single measurement. It is optimal only for linear systems with Gaussian noise, and when the model is wrong the failure mode is confident and wrong.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 16.322 Stochastic Estimation and Control (discrete- and continuous-time Kalman filtering) https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/16-322-stochastic-estimation-and-control-fall-2004/pages/syllabus
candidates.overlapWith: feedback-control: that page corrects an actuator from an error signal; this page estimates the state the controller needs from noisy measurements, and the two are usually paired in a real robot.

candidates.title: Shannon's limit
candidates.interaction: Send bits through a channel that flips each one with probability p and try to get the message across: repetition codes trade rate for errors along one curve, while random block codes with a long block push the error toward zero at any rate below 1 minus H(p) and fail above it, with the measured points landing on either side of the capacity line. Switch to a noisy analogue channel: set bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio, see the capacity curve, and overlay the constellations of the wireless page to see how close real schemes get.
candidates.takeaway: Every noisy channel has a hard ceiling on how fast information can cross it without error, and below that ceiling the errors can be driven as low as you like.
candidates.pitfall: Capacity is not the error-free rate of any particular code; it is a limit approached only with long codes and delay. It is set by bandwidth and signal-to-noise together, so doubling the power does not double the rate.
candidates.why: MIT OCW 6.451 Principles of Digital Communication II: 'coding techniques that approach the Shannon limit', capacity of AWGN channels https://videolectures.net/mit6451s05_principles_digital_communication
candidates.overlapWith: error-correction: that page repairs single-bit errors with one code; this page asks how good any code can ever be, and shows the answer is a single number the graphic can reach.

candidates.title: Video compression
candidates.interaction: Step through encoding a short clip: each frame is cut into blocks, every block searches the previous frame for its best match and keeps only a motion vector and the difference, which is transformed and quantised like the JPEG blocks of the compression page. Scrub the quality and the search range and watch bits per frame fall while blocking and smearing appear; corrupt one keyframe and see the damage propagate until the next.
candidates.takeaway: A video is mostly its previous frame moved a little, so a codec sends motion and the leftovers, and almost none of the pixels.
candidates.needs: A few seconds of Big Buck Bunny frames (Blender Foundation, CC BY 3.0), video only: the film's score is CC BY-NC-ND and must not be shipped.
candidates.pitfall: Motion vectors are not object tracking: each is whichever block matched best, which is why they look chaotic on textures. The decoder must reconstruct exactly what the encoder predicted from, or the drift compounds frame after frame.
candidates.why: Demand: Google 'how does video compression work' https://www.google.com/search?q=how+does+video+compression+work (the Stanford EE398A Image and Video Compression course page was not fetched this session, the search budget ran out)
candidates.overlapWith: compression: that page compresses one still image by discarding high frequencies; this page adds time, prediction from the previous frame, which is where almost all the saving comes from.
candidates.needsSource: Big Buck Bunny frames, CC BY 3.0 (openly licensed; audio excluded)

candidates.title: Sampling & perceptual audio coding
candidates.interaction: Sample a tone at an adjustable rate and watch it alias into a lower pitch once the rate drops below twice its frequency, then reconstruct the samples with sinc interpolation and reduce the bit depth until quantisation noise shows on the spectrum. Load a short clip: the page computes its spectrum frame by frame, draws a masking threshold around the loud components and drops everything beneath it; a slider trades bits against audible damage, shown on the spectrogram and in the bit count.
candidates.takeaway: Digital audio can be perfect below half the sampling rate, and most of what a recording contains is sound the ear would never notice, so a codec throws it away.
candidates.needs: A short CC0 music or speech clip (Wikimedia Commons or Freesound CC0). The masking model must be a published simplification (a spreading-function model as in Johnston 1988), stated on the page, because the MPEG psychoacoustic model lives in an ISO standard that is not open; that makes this the weaker of the two codec candidates.
candidates.pitfall: Sampling loses nothing below the Nyquist frequency, so 'digital sound is steppy' is wrong. Perceptual coding is lossy by design: what is dropped is gone, not hidden somewhere.
candidates.why: MIT 6.003 Signals and Systems, Lecture 22 'Sampling and quantization' https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-003-signals-and-systems-fall-2011/resources/mit6_003f11_lec22/ (the sampling-theorem seed is folded in here)

candidates.title: Tor & onion routing
candidates.interaction: Pick a guard, a middle and an exit relay on a map and watch a message be wrapped in three layers of encryption and peeled one layer per hop; click any relay to see what it alone can learn (the guard knows you, the exit knows the destination, the middle knows neither). Give an observer control of some fraction of the relays and run many circuits to see how often one observer sees both ends; then let a global observer correlate the timing of packets at both ends anyway.
candidates.takeaway: Routing through three relays with layered encryption means no single point knows both who is talking and to whom, and the protection is only as good as the share of relays an adversary does not control.
candidates.pitfall: Tor hides who is talking to whom, not what is said at the exit: traffic to a plain HTTP site is readable by the exit relay. It is not a VPN with extra hops; a VPN is one party who knows everything.

candidates.title: Distributed hash tables & consistent hashing
candidates.interaction: Hash keys and servers onto a ring and watch a lookup walk around it; add or remove a server and count how many keys move, with consistent hashing against the naive modulo rule. Then give each node a finger table and watch lookups finish in a number of hops that grows only logarithmically as the network grows to thousands of nodes; churn nodes in and out and see the ring heal or lose keys depending on how many replicas each key has.
candidates.takeaway: Thousands of machines can find any key among them in a dozen hops with no directory, and adding one machine moves only its own share of the keys.
candidates.pitfall: Consistent hashing is not fair by default: with one point per server the loads vary widely, which is what virtual nodes fix. A DHT finds where a key lives; it does not make the data durable, replication does.

candidates.title: Version control & Merkle trees
candidates.interaction: Edit files in a toy repository and commit; the page hashes each file, each directory and each commit and draws the resulting graph of content-addressed objects, where two identical files are one object. Branch, make conflicting edits and merge: the three-way merge runs a real diff algorithm on each file and shows where it has to ask you. Change one byte in an old commit and watch every hash above it change, then verify one file's membership with a Merkle proof whose size grows only with the logarithm of the tree.
candidates.takeaway: Naming every piece of data by the hash of its contents makes history tamper-evident and lets two copies prove they agree by comparing one hash.

candidates.needsSource: Fashion-MNIST, MIT licence (confirmed) for the precomputed image samples; own weights.

candidates.title: Normalizing flows
candidates.interaction: Stack invertible layers (an affine coupling layer, a rotation, an elementwise squash) and drag their parameters: a grid drawn on the plane warps, and the Gaussian base density is recolored by the exact change-of-variables rule, dense where the map squeezes space and thin where it stretches it. Then train the stack on two-moons data and watch the Gaussian flow into the data; run it backwards to see samples born from noise.
candidates.takeaway: A chain of invertible maps with a cheap Jacobian is a generative model whose likelihood is exact: the density at a point is the base density at its preimage times how much the map shrank space there.
candidates.pitfall: The log-determinant must come from the layer structure (coupling layers make the Jacobian triangular); estimating the density from sample histograms is exactly what flows avoid. Say that flow matching is a different, later idea.
candidates.why: Stanford CS236 Deep Generative Models covers flow models alongside VAEs and GANs: https://bulletin.stanford.edu/courses/2205691
candidates.overlapWith: linear-transformations: that page warps a grid with one 2x2 matrix; here nonlinear invertible layers warp a probability density and the determinant becomes a likelihood.

candidates.title: RLHF: learning from human preferences
candidates.interaction: Read pairs of continuations that a real small language model wrote for a prompt and click the better one; a reward model (a linear layer on each continuation's sentence embedding, fit by the Bradley-Terry rule) updates after every click and scores all the candidates. Slide the KL penalty: the policy, computed exactly as the base model's distribution tilted by exp(reward/beta), drifts from the base model toward the reward model's favourites, and with a small penalty it collapses onto whichever odd continuation the reward model over-rates, reward hacking visible in the ranked list.
candidates.takeaway: Comparisons train a reward model, and the policy is the base model's distribution pulled toward that reward and held back by a KL leash; loosen the leash and the policy exploits the reward model's mistakes instead of the preferences behind them.
candidates.needs: For a handful of prompts, about 64 sampled continuations each with reference log-probabilities from GPT-2 small (OpenAI, modified MIT licence) and one sentence embedding per continuation from an open embedding model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Apache 2.0), all precomputed.
candidates.pitfall: RLHF teaches no new facts; it reweights outputs the base model could already produce. On a finite candidate set the KL-regularized optimum is closed-form, so the page must not pretend PPO is running; say that DPO uses the same closed form.
candidates.why: Hugging Face, Illustrating RLHF (reward model, KL penalty): https://huggingface.co/blog/rlhf ; Stanford CS224N has an RLHF lecture (slide archive https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs224n/cs224n.1246/slides/).
candidates.overlapWith: reinforcement-learning: that page learns values from rewards painted on a grid; here the reward itself is learned from comparisons and the environment is a language model's own output distribution.
candidates.needsSource: GPT-2 weights, OpenAI modified MIT (confirmed); all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Apache 2.0 (from memory, unverified); the continuations and labels are generated by the project.

candidates.title: Mixture of experts
candidates.interaction: Assemble a layer from a palette of small expert networks and a router, set how many experts each input may use, and train it on a 2-D regression: the plane is tiled by which expert each input is routed to, each expert's own fit is drawn in its tile, and a histogram counts inputs per expert. Remove the load-balancing loss and watch one expert take every input while the others idle; a counter shows parameters stored against parameters used per input.
candidates.takeaway: A router sends each input to a few of many experts, so a model can hold far more parameters than it spends per token, and routing collapses onto one expert unless a balancing term pushes traffic apart.
candidates.pitfall: Experts do not specialize by topic as the name suggests; in real language models they split by token-level patterns. The top-k choice is discrete, so show that the gate's softmax weight is what carries the gradient.
candidates.why: Hugging Face, Mixture of Experts Explained: https://huggingface.co/blog/moe
candidates.overlapWith: transformers: that page shows attention mixing tokens; this one replaces the feed-forward block with routed experts and shows the compute-per-token against total-parameters trade.

candidates.title: Tokenization & byte-pair encoding
candidates.interaction: Type a small corpus and run byte-pair encoding one merge at a time: the most frequent adjacent pair fuses, the vocabulary grows by one and the token count of a sample sentence falls, plotted as a curve. Then type any text and watch GPT-2's real byte-level tokenizer apply its merges in rank order after the regex pre-split: common English words become one token, a rare word breaks into several pieces, numbers split oddly, and the same sentence in another language or script costs far more tokens.
candidates.takeaway: Tokens are greedy merges of the most frequent byte pairs in the training text, so a model sees whole words where text is common and fragments where it is rare, and never sees letters.
candidates.needs: GPT-2's merge list and vocabulary (OpenAI; shipped by tiktoken under MIT, the GPT-2 release under a modified MIT licence).
candidates.pitfall: Merges apply in rank order, not by longest match, so the split is deterministic given the merge list; byte-level BPE never needs an unknown token. Do not say that models count letters.
candidates.why: Hugging Face NLP course, chapter 6, byte-pair encoding tokenization: https://huggingface.co/learn/nlp-course/chapter6/5
candidates.overlapWith: language-models: that page splits typed text into tokens as given; this one builds the tokenizer merge by merge and shows why the split falls where it does.
candidates.needsSource: tiktoken, MIT (confirmed); the GPT-2 merge and vocabulary files sit in OpenAI's gpt-2 repository under its modified MIT licence (repository licence; the files were not separately checked).

candidates.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
candidates.interaction: Assemble a retrieval pipeline over a few thousand Simple English Wikipedia paragraphs: choose the chunk size, keyword (BM25) or embedding search and how many chunks to keep, then type a question and watch the chunks ranked live with their scores and the prompt assembled from them. For a fixed set of questions, flip between the model's precomputed answer with and without the retrieved chunks and see the answer follow the chunks: right when the fact was retrieved, fluently wrong when it was not.
candidates.takeaway: A language model can only use what is in its prompt, so retrieval decides what it can quote, and the chunking and ranking, not the model, is where most answers are won or lost.
candidates.needs: A Simple English Wikipedia extract (CC BY-SA 4.0); embeddings computed in the browser or precomputed with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Apache 2.0); precomputed answers from a small openly licensed model (an Apache-2.0 Qwen or SmolLM checkpoint).
candidates.pitfall: Retrieval does not make a model truthful; it will quote a wrong chunk fluently. Keyword and dense search fail on different questions, so show both.
candidates.why: Lewis et al. 2020, Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
candidates.overlapWith: embeddings: that page finds the nearest words in vector space; this one feeds the nearest passages to a generator and shows the generation change.
candidates.needsSource: Simple English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0; all-MiniLM-L6-v2, Apache 2.0 (from memory, unverified); answer model licence to confirm when chosen.

candidates.title: Decision trees, random forests & gradient boosting
candidates.interaction: Grow a decision tree one split at a time on 2-D points or on the Palmer penguins: each candidate split's impurity drop is shown, the chosen one slices the plane, and the tree deepens until it has memorized every point. Then bag many trees trained on bootstrap resamples and watch the jagged boundary average smooth, and finally boost: each new shallow tree fits the current residuals and the sum of trees staircases toward the data, with the learning rate and depth as sliders and the test error plotted.
candidates.takeaway: A single tree slices the plane greedily and overfits, averaging many resampled trees cancels their noise, and boosting adds small trees that each fix what the ensemble still gets wrong.
candidates.needs: Palmer penguins dataset (Horst, Hill and Gorman; CC0).
candidates.pitfall: A random forest does not overfit by adding trees; boosting does. Impurity-based feature importance is biased toward high-cardinality features and is not causal.
candidates.why: Stanford CS229 summer 2020 syllabus covers decision trees, random forests and gradient boosting as tree ensembles: https://cs229.stanford.edu/summer2020/syllabus.html
candidates.overlapWith: learning-from-data: that page fits one polynomial of growing degree; here axis-aligned splits grow a tree and the ensemble steps, bagging and boosting, are the content.
candidates.needsSource: Palmer penguins, CC0 (from memory, unverified in this session).

candidates.title: Support vector machines & kernels
candidates.interaction: Drag labeled points on the plane: a perceptron finds some separating line, then the SVM finds the one with the widest margin, with the support vectors highlighted and every other point free to move without changing it. Lower the penalty C to let points inside the margin, then switch on a polynomial or Gaussian kernel and drag its width to see the straight margin in feature space land as a curved boundary on the plane.
candidates.takeaway: The best separating line is the one farthest from the nearest points, which alone determine it, and a kernel lets the same margin-maximizer draw curves by measuring similarity instead of coordinates.
candidates.pitfall: The kernel trick never computes the high-dimensional features; the solution depends on the data only through inner products. Kernel width and C trade off flexibility against margin, not accuracy against speed.
candidates.why: Stanford CS229 fall 2021 syllabus, lectures on support vector machines and kernels: https://cs229.stanford.edu/syllabus-fall2021.html
candidates.overlapWith: neural-networks: that page learns a boundary by backpropagation; here the boundary solves a convex margin problem decided by a few points, and the kernel takes the place of hidden layers.

candidates.title: Clustering: k-means & Gaussian mixtures
candidates.interaction: Scatter points or load the Palmer penguins without their labels and step k-means: assign each point to its nearest centre, move the centres, repeat; try several k and seeds and watch it fail on elongated clusters. Switch to expectation-maximization on a Gaussian mixture, where each point is colored by its soft responsibilities, the ellipses stretch to fit and the log-likelihood climbs; then watch a density-based method pick out a ring that both of the others cut in half.
candidates.takeaway: Clustering is fitting a model of groups without labels, and each algorithm's idea of a group, nearest centre, Gaussian blob or dense region, decides what it can and cannot find.
candidates.needs: Palmer penguins dataset (CC0).
candidates.pitfall: k-means returns k clusters whether or not they exist, so show it carving a single blob; EM finds a local maximum that depends on the start.
candidates.why: Stanford CS229 fall 2021 syllabus, k-means, expectation-maximization and mixtures of Gaussians: https://cs229.stanford.edu/syllabus-fall2021.html
candidates.overlapWith: learning-from-data: that page fits labeled points; here there are no labels and the algorithm's assumption about group shape is what is on display.
candidates.needsSource: Palmer penguins, CC0 (from memory, unverified in this session).

candidates.title: Dimensionality reduction: PCA & t-SNE
candidates.interaction: Rotate a 3-D cloud of points and watch its shadow on the screen: the principal axes are the rotation that keeps the most spread, and dropping the third axis loses the least. Then run t-SNE live on a few hundred clothing images: the map forms as the gradient steps run, and sliding the perplexity or reseeding rearranges it, which shows what is real (who neighbours whom) and what is an artefact (cluster sizes and the gaps between them).
candidates.takeaway: PCA keeps the directions of largest variance and nothing else, while t-SNE keeps each point's neighbours and sacrifices everything else, so the two maps answer different questions.
candidates.needs: A Fashion-MNIST subset (MIT).
candidates.pitfall: Distances between t-SNE clusters and their sizes mean nothing; the page must not read them. Principal components are directions of variance, not the features that matter for a task.
candidates.why: Distill, How to Use t-SNE Effectively: https://distill.pub/2016/misread-tsne/
candidates.overlapWith: embeddings: that page's pitfall warns that its 2-D map distorts distances; this page is about how such maps are made and exactly what each one distorts.

candidates.title: Bayesian inference & MCMC
candidates.interaction: Choose a posterior you can only evaluate up to a constant (a banana, a donut, or the posterior of a logistic regression on a few points) and release a Metropolis random walk: each proposal is drawn and accepted or rejected with its ratio shown, and the trace and histogram fill in. Tune the step size, too small crawls and too large rejects, then switch to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and watch a particle glide along the contours with far fewer rejections.
candidates.takeaway: You can sample a distribution you cannot normalize by a random walk that always accepts uphill and sometimes accepts downhill, and the chain's histogram becomes the posterior; how fast depends on how the proposals are made.
candidates.pitfall: Early samples are burn-in and consecutive samples are correlated; do not present the chain as independent draws, and do not present the acceptance rate as a quality score.
candidates.why: Chi Feng's interactive MCMC gallery, featured by Andrew Gelman: https://andrewgelman.com/2018/07/26/awesome-mcmc-animation-site-chi-feng-github/
candidates.overlapWith: bayes-theorem: that page does one update by counting a grid of people; here the parameter is continuous, the posterior cannot be written down and the computation that recovers it is the content.

candidates.title: Gaussian processes
candidates.interaction: Click to add observations on a blank axis and watch the posterior mean and its 95% band snap to them with sample functions drawn through; the band pinches to nothing at the data and swells between points. Drag the kernel's length scale and noise, swap kernels (squared exponential, periodic, linear) with the kernel matrix shown as a heat map alongside, then let the page choose the next point to query by upper confidence bound, the step at the heart of Bayesian optimization.
candidates.takeaway: A Gaussian process is a distribution over functions set by a kernel, and conditioning it on data pins it down where observed and leaves uncertainty that grows with distance from the data at a rate the kernel sets.
candidates.pitfall: Draw sample functions, not only the mean and band; the mean alone looks like any smoother. The band's width away from data comes from the prior, not from evidence.
candidates.why: Rasmussen and Williams, Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning, the standard text, free online: https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/
candidates.overlapWith: learning-from-data: that page fits one curve; here the fit is a whole distribution of curves and the uncertainty between data points is the point.

candidates.title: Graph neural networks
candidates.interaction: On Zachary's karate club (34 members, two factions) label two members and step message passing one layer at a time: each node's vector becomes an aggregate of its neighbours', drawn as a 2-D embedding that moves at every layer, and the faction prediction spreads outward from the two seeds. Keep stacking layers and watch every embedding converge to one point, then show two different graphs that every such network embeds identically.
candidates.takeaway: A graph network updates each node from its neighbours' messages, so after k layers a node summarizes its k-hop neighbourhood, and with too many layers every node summarizes the same thing.
candidates.needs: Zachary's karate-club graph (34 nodes, Table 3 of Zachary 1977, redistributed with NetworkX).
candidates.pitfall: Message passing is not PageRank: the aggregation weights are learned. The Weisfeiler-Lehman limit means some non-isomorphic graphs are indistinguishable to message passing, and the page should show a pair.
candidates.why: Stanford CS224W 2023 slides on message passing and GNN expressive power: https://snap.stanford.edu/class/cs224w-2023/slides/07-theory.pdf
candidates.overlapWith: pagerank: that page propagates a scalar along links by a fixed rule; here vectors propagate with learned weights, and oversmoothing and the expressiveness limit are new.
candidates.needsSource: Zachary karate club: 34-node table from a 1977 paper, widely redistributed, licence unverified; trivially small and could be re-entered from the paper with citation.

candidates.title: Speech recognition: from sound to letters
candidates.interaction: Pick a one-second spoken word from the Speech Commands set, or say one into the microphone, and step it through the pipeline: waveform, spectrogram, mel features, then a small network's per-frame letter probabilities drawn as a lattice. Watch connectionist temporal classification collapse the frames, repeats and blanks, into the word, and drag the alignment to see why the model never needs to know where each letter starts.
candidates.takeaway: Speech recognition turns a spectrogram into a letter probability per time slice and then collapses repeats and blanks, so the network is never told where each sound begins and ends.
candidates.needs: A subset of Google's Speech Commands v2 (CC BY 4.0, with a no-speaker-identification condition) and a small CTC model trained on it offline (own weights).
candidates.pitfall: This is isolated-word recognition; continuous speech adds a language model and beam-search decoding, say so. Do not say the network hears phonemes.
candidates.why: Speech Commands dataset card, CC BY 4.0: https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/speech_commands ; Stanford CS224S Spoken Language Processing covers CTC.
candidates.overlapWith: fourier-transform: that page turns a signal into frequencies; this one continues from the spectrogram to letters and shows the CTC alignment.
candidates.needsSource: Google Speech Commands v2, CC BY 4.0 (confirmed); own trained weights.

candidates.title: Recommender systems & collaborative filtering
candidates.interaction: Rate a dozen films and watch a matrix-factorization model, two hidden factors per person and per film fit by alternating least squares live, place you and the films on a 2-D map and fill in your blank ratings. Add factors and regularization and see the held-out error curve; add a new film with no ratings and see cold start, and watch popularity bias as the most-rated films are recommended to everyone.
candidates.takeaway: Recommendations come from factoring the sparse ratings table into a few hidden tastes per person and per item, so people who rated like you did are your prediction, and an item nobody has rated cannot be placed.
candidates.needs: A ratings dataset. MovieLens ml-latest-small (GroupLens) permits redistribution only under its research, non-commercial conditions, which is not an open licence; this candidate's data is weak unless an openly licensed ratings set is found.
candidates.pitfall: The factors are not genres; do not name them. Held-out ratings are a biased test because people choose what to rate.
candidates.why: Stanford CS246 Mining Massive Data Sets, recommender systems lectures: http://web.stanford.edu/class/cs246/ ; MovieLens terms: https://files.grouplens.org/datasets/movielens/ml-latest-small-README.html
candidates.overlapWith: embeddings: that page maps words from pretrained vectors; here the vectors are learned live from a ratings table and the problem is the missing entries.
candidates.needsSource: MovieLens ml-latest-small: research-only, non-commercial redistribution terms (confirmed), not an open licence; weak.

candidates.title: Evolutionary algorithms
candidates.interaction: Release a population on the landscapes gradient descent uses, plus a jagged one with no useful gradient: CMA-ES draws its population as an ellipse that stretches along the valley and shrinks as it converges, with mutation strength and population size as sliders. Then run a genetic algorithm on a discrete problem, a short tour through cities, with crossover, mutation and selection pressure as controls, and watch diversity collapse when selection is too strong.
candidates.takeaway: A population under selection, mutation and recombination can climb a landscape with no gradient at all, and the spread of the population is the search's memory of which directions worked.
candidates.pitfall: Evolutionary search is an optimizer, not a model of biology; fitness is a function the designer chose. Do not present the genetic algorithm as the method of choice: CMA-ES is what is used on continuous problems.
candidates.why: David Ha, A Visual Guide to Evolution Strategies: https://blog.otoro.net/2017/10/29/visual-evolution-strategies/
candidates.overlapWith: evolution: that page shows natural selection acting on creatures at level 1; here selection, mutation and recombination are optimizers on a fitness landscape, compared with gradient descent.

candidates.title: Bias, variance & double descent
candidates.interaction: Fit random-feature ridge regression to noisy data and slide the number of features from a few to many times the number of points: the test error rises, peaks exactly where the model can first fit every point, then falls again, while the training error hits zero and stays there. Resample the training set many times to see the fits' spread (variance) and their average's miss (bias), add label noise to sharpen the peak, and add ridge regularization to erase it.
candidates.takeaway: Test error peaks where a model has just enough parameters to memorize its data and falls again beyond it, so models larger than their data can generalize, and regularization smooths the peak away.
candidates.pitfall: The classical U-shaped curve is not wrong, it is the left half. The second descent needs the minimum-norm (or implicitly regularized) solution; with an arbitrary interpolating fit it does not happen.
candidates.why: OpenAI, Deep Double Descent (Nakkiran et al. 2019): https://openai.com/index/deep-double-descent
candidates.overlapWith: learning-from-data: that page stops where the test error turns upward; this one keeps adding parameters through the interpolation peak and down the other side.

candidates.title: Dropout, weight decay & batch normalization
candidates.interaction: Build a small network on a 2-D dataset from a palette that includes dropout and batch-norm layers and train it live: the decision boundary, the weight histogram and each layer's activation distribution update as it learns. Switch dropout on to see many thinned sub-networks' boundaries and their average; add weight decay and watch the weights shrink and the boundary smooth; add batch norm, raise the learning rate tenfold and see the activations stay centred where the plain network's blow up.
candidates.takeaway: Dropout trains an ensemble of thinned networks at once, weight decay keeps the function smooth, and batch norm keeps each layer's inputs in range so training survives large steps.
candidates.pitfall: Dropout is off at test time with activations rescaled, and batch norm behaves differently in training and inference; the page must show both modes. Do not state that batch norm works by removing internal covariate shift as established fact.
candidates.why: Stanford CS231n, lecture Training Neural Networks (dropout, batch normalization, weight decay): https://cs231n.stanford.edu/schedule.html
candidates.overlapWith: neural-networks: that page builds and trains plain layers; this one adds the regularizers and the normalization and shows what each does to the weights and activations.

candidates.title: Momentum, Adam & learning-rate schedules
candidates.interaction: Race plain gradient descent, momentum, RMSProp and Adam on a bowl whose condition number you set with a slider: stretch it a thousand to one and watch plain descent zigzag or stall while Adam's per-parameter step sizes, drawn as arrows, rescale the long axis. Tune momentum past critical damping to see it oscillate, then add warmup and a cosine schedule and compare how each optimizer finishes on a small real network's loss curve.
candidates.takeaway: Gradient descent is slow when the loss is stretched more along some parameters than others, and momentum, per-parameter scaling and schedules each fix a different part of that.
candidates.pitfall: Adam does not find better minima, it reaches them faster, and on some problems plain momentum generalizes better; do not declare a winner. The momentum analysis is exact only for quadratics, say so.
candidates.why: Distill, Why Momentum Really Works (Goh 2017): https://distill.pub/2017/momentum/
candidates.overlapWith: gradient-descent: that page already offers a momentum toggle on ravines and plateaus; here the ravine's conditioning is the control, and per-parameter scaling (RMSProp, Adam) and schedules are new.

candidates.title: Scaling laws
candidates.interaction: Scrub a precomputed sweep of small networks trained with growing width and data on one task and watch the loss fall as a straight line on log-log axes until the data or the model runs out, then retrain one point of the sweep live and see it land on the line. Switch to the Chinchilla parametric law and drag a compute budget: the page solves for the model size and token count that minimize the fitted loss, drawing the iso-compute curves and the optimal frontier.
candidates.takeaway: Loss falls as a power law in model size and in data, each saturating when the other is the bottleneck, so a given compute budget has an optimal split between the two.
candidates.needs: The project's own precomputed sweep of small models; the Chinchilla fit L = E + A/N^a + B/D^b with the constants published by Hoffmann et al. 2022; optionally Epoch AI's re-extracted data points.
candidates.pitfall: Scaling laws are empirical fits with disputed constants (Epoch AI's replication); do not present them as physics. The live retrain must be tiny and labelled as such, not a per-slider sweep.
candidates.why: Hoffmann et al. 2022, Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15556 ; Epoch AI replication: https://epoch.ai/publications/chinchilla-scaling-a-replication-attempt
candidates.overlapWith: language-models: that page shows what a trained model does; this one shows how its loss depends on size and data and why models are the sizes they are.
candidates.needsSource: Own sweep (none external); Chinchilla constants are published numbers (arXiv paper, licence not checked); Epoch AI extracted data, licence unverified.

candidates.title: Superposition & sparse autoencoders
candidates.interaction: Train Anthropic's toy model live: more features than hidden neurons, each feature active with a sparsity you set; the learned feature directions are drawn in the hidden plane and go from only the most important features, at right angles, to all of them packed as antipodal pairs and pentagons as the features grow sparser. Then train a sparse autoencoder on the hidden activations and watch its dictionary recover the packed directions one by one.
candidates.takeaway: A network can store more features than it has neurons by overlapping them when features are rarely active together, and a sparse autoencoder can pull the overlapped features apart again.
candidates.pitfall: Neurons are not features, so do not label individual hidden units. Sparse-autoencoder features are a hypothesis about the model, not ground truth, and the toy model's results do not transfer wholesale to real networks.
candidates.why: Anthropic, Toy Models of Superposition: https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/toy_model/index.html ; DeepMind's Gemma Scope release of open SAEs: https://deepmind.google/blog/gemma-scope-helping-the-safety-community-shed-light-on-the-inner-workings-of-language-models/
candidates.overlapWith: embeddings: that page shows meaning as directions in a vector space; here the question is how many directions fit in one layer and how to recover them from a trained network.
candidates.needsSource: none (the toy model and the sparse autoencoder train in the browser)

candidates.title: Induction heads & in-context learning
candidates.interaction: Scrub through the training run of a tiny two-layer attention-only transformer trained on repeated random token sequences (checkpoints precomputed): the loss on the second copy of each sequence drops suddenly at one point of training, and hovering any token shows the attention pattern at that checkpoint. Before the drop the heads attend diffusely; after it, one head in the first layer attends to the previous token and one in the second attends to the token that followed the current token's last occurrence, and ablating either head erases the drop live.
candidates.takeaway: In-context copying is done by a two-head circuit, a previous-token head feeding an induction head, and it appears abruptly during training, which is why the loss curve has a step.
candidates.needs: The project's own precomputed checkpoints of a tiny attention-only transformer (a vocabulary of tens of tokens, two layers), run in the browser.
candidates.pitfall: The circuit is established in small attention-only models; in large models the evidence is correlational, say so. Attention weights are not explanations on their own; the ablation is the evidence.
candidates.why: Anthropic, In-context Learning and Induction Heads (Olsson et al. 2022): https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads/index.html
candidates.overlapWith: transformers: that page shows a trained model's attention on sentences; this one shows a circuit of two heads forming during training and tests it by ablation.

candidates.title: Recurrent networks & LSTMs
candidates.interaction: Feed a sequence symbol by symbol into a plain recurrent network and an LSTM trained to recall its first symbol after a gap you set: the hidden state and the LSTM's forget, input and output gates are drawn at each step. Then run backpropagation through time and watch the gradient reaching the early steps shrink geometrically in the plain network while the LSTM's cell state carries it almost unchanged; lengthen the gap until the plain network fails and the LSTM still works.
candidates.takeaway: A recurrent network carries a state from step to step, and gates that choose what to keep let a signal, and its gradient, travel far back through time without vanishing.
candidates.pitfall: Vanishing gradients come from repeated multiplication by the same Jacobian, not from forgetting; show the gradient norms, not a metaphor. LSTMs mitigate the problem, they do not remove it, and saturated gates stop learning.
candidates.why: MIT 6.S191 2025, lecture 2 Deep Sequence Modeling (RNNs, LSTMs): https://introtodeeplearning.com/2025/index.html
candidates.overlapWith: transformers: that page mixes all tokens at once with attention; here the model is sequential with a carried state and the question is how far a signal survives.

candidates.title: Contrastive & self-supervised learning
candidates.interaction: Train a small encoder on unlabeled clothing images where the only signal is agreement: two random augmentations (crop, flip, blur) of the same image are pulled together on a unit circle of embeddings and all other images are pushed apart. Watch the circle sort itself into clothing types without ever seeing a label, slide the temperature to make the negatives push harder or softer, then flip to the CLIP variant where a grid of image-text similarities is trained to light up only on its diagonal.
candidates.takeaway: A representation can be learned with no labels by making a network agree with itself across augmentations and disagree with other examples, and the augmentations decide what the representation learns to ignore.
candidates.needs: A Fashion-MNIST subset (MIT); the encoder trains live or is scrubbed from precomputed checkpoints (own weights).
candidates.pitfall: Self-supervised is not unsupervised clustering: the augmentations are a design choice that injects knowledge. Collapse, every embedding equal, is the failure to show.
candidates.why: Chen et al. 2020, SimCLR, A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations: https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05709
candidates.overlapWith: embeddings: that page explores a given embedding space; this one shows how such a space is trained without labels.

candidates.title: Adversarial examples
candidates.interaction: Draw a digit for a small classifier running in the browser, then drag an epsilon slider: the page adds epsilon times the sign of the loss gradient, an image you can see beside the digit, and the prediction flips from 3 to 8 while the drawn digit looks unchanged. Compare a random perturbation of the same size, which does nothing, then switch to a model trained adversarially and see the flip need a visible epsilon and the clean accuracy fall.
candidates.takeaway: Because a classifier is nearly linear in its input, a tiny step along the gradient of its loss, invisible to the eye, flips its output, while random noise of the same size does not.
candidates.needs: A small digit classifier with backpropagation to the input in the browser, trained on MNIST (CC BY-SA 3.0) as the existing convolution-vision page's drawn-digit classifier is, plus an adversarially trained twin; the page ships only its own weights, no images.
candidates.pitfall: Adversarial examples are not a bug of one model; they transfer between models trained separately. The perturbation is not noise, and robustness is bought with clean accuracy.
candidates.why: Goodfellow, Shlens and Szegedy 2015, Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples: https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.6572
candidates.overlapWith: convolution-vision: that page inspects what a classifier responds to; this one attacks the same kind of classifier through its gradient.
candidates.needsSource: MNIST, CC BY-SA 3.0 (confirmed); only own trained weights are shipped, following the data decision of convolution-vision.

candidates.title: Federated learning & differential privacy
candidates.interaction: Split a 2-D dataset across several devices, each holding its own skewed slice, and run federated averaging: every device trains locally for a few steps, sends its update, and the server averages them into one model whose boundary is drawn on every device. Make the slices more unlike each other and watch client drift pull the average off course; then clip each update and add noise with a privacy budget slider and see the accuracy paid for every notch of privacy.
candidates.takeaway: A model can be trained without the data leaving the devices by averaging their updates, and the privacy of each update is bought with clipping and noise that cost accuracy.
candidates.pitfall: Federated learning alone is not private: gradients can leak training data, which is why differential privacy is added. Epsilon is a bound on how much one person's data can change the output, not a probability of a leak.
candidates.why: McMahan et al. 2017, Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data: https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.05629
candidates.overlapWith: neural-networks: that page trains on one dataset in one place; here the data is split over devices, averaging is the mechanism and privacy noise is the trade.

candidates.title: Monte Carlo tree search & AlphaGo
candidates.interaction: Play Connect Four against the page and step its thinking one simulation at a time: selection walks down the tree by the upper-confidence rule, expansion adds a node, a random rollout plays the game to the end, and the result is backed up as visit counts and win rates, so the tree grows lopsided toward promising moves. Set the simulation budget and the exploration constant, then replace the random rollouts with a small value and policy network trained by self-play and see the same budget play far better.
candidates.takeaway: Tree search can play well with no rules of thumb by sampling games and growing the tree where the samples look best, and a learned value network in place of random rollouts is the AlphaGo idea.
candidates.needs: None for the search itself; a small Connect Four policy and value network trained by self-play offline (own weights).
candidates.pitfall: MCTS is not minimax with random tie-breaking; the asymmetric growth is the point. AlphaGo's networks did not replace search, they guided it.
candidates.why: Silver et al. 2016, Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search, Nature: https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16961
candidates.overlapWith: graph-search: that page finds shortest paths in a known graph; here the tree is grown by sampling under uncertainty and value estimates decide where it grows.

candidates.title: World models & model-based RL
candidates.interaction: Let an agent act in a small physical world (a cart balancing a pole) while a small network learns to predict the next state from the current state and action; imagined rollouts are drawn as ghosts over the real ones and drift apart as the horizon grows. Slide the number of planning steps taken in imagination per real step and watch the learning curve steepen, then lengthen the imagined horizon until compounding model error has the agent planning for a world that does not exist.
candidates.takeaway: Learning a model of the world lets an agent practice in imagination, which buys sample efficiency as long as imagined rollouts stay shorter than the horizon at which the model's errors compound.
candidates.pitfall: A world model is not the true physics; show its error growing with horizon. Model-based learning is not always more sample-efficient, and a wrong model can make the agent worse than model-free learning.
candidates.why: Berkeley CS285 fall 2023, lectures 10 to 12 on planning and model-based RL: https://rail.eecs.berkeley.edu/deeprlcourse-fa23/ ; Ha and Schmidhuber 2018, World Models: https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.10122
candidates.overlapWith: reinforcement-learning: that page learns values by trial in a grid world; here the agent learns the world's dynamics and plans inside the learned model.

candidates.title: Confidence & calibration
candidates.interaction: Train a small classifier on 2-D data and paint its confidence over the plane: it is near certain far from any data, where it has no business being sure. A reliability diagram bins predictions by confidence against how often they are right; drag a temperature slider to rescale the logits and watch the diagram straighten and the calibration error fall, then switch on an ensemble of five networks and see the far-away confidence finally drop where the members disagree.
candidates.takeaway: A network's softmax confidence is not its probability of being right; one temperature can fix the calibration on data like the training data, but only disagreement between models reveals where there is no data at all.
candidates.pitfall: Temperature scaling changes no predicted class and no accuracy: calibration and accuracy are different things, and a calibrated model can still be confidently wrong off-distribution.
candidates.why: Guo et al. 2017, On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks: https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.04599
candidates.overlapWith: gaussian-processes: that page's uncertainty comes from a prior over functions; here it is a trained classifier's confidence and how to correct it.
